מַר רַבִּי יוּדָן בְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן כָּל בְּהֵמוֹת וְלִוְיָתָן הֵן קֶנִיגִין שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא, וְכָל מִי שֶׁלֹּא רָאָה קֶנִיגִין שֶׁל אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, זוֹכֶה לִרְאוֹתָהּ לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, כֵּיצַד הֵם נִשְׁחָטִים, בְּהֵמוֹת נוֹתֵץ לַלִּוְיָתָן בְּקַרְנָיו וְקוֹרְעוֹ, וְלִוְיָתָן נוֹתֵץ לַבְּהֵמוֹת בִּסְנַפִּירָיו וְנוֹחֲרוֹ. וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים זוֹ שְׁחִיטָה כְּשֵׁרָה הִיא, וְלֹא כָּךְ תָּנִינַן הַכֹּל שׁוֹחֲטִין וּבַכֹּל שׁוֹחֲטִין וּלְעוֹלָם שׁוֹחֲטִין חוּץ מִמַּגַּל קָצִיר, וְהַמְגֵרָה, וְהַשִּׁנַּיִם, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהֵן חוֹנְקִין. אָמַר רַבִּי אָבִין בַּר כַּהֲנָא אָמַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא (ישעיה נא, ד): תּוֹרָה חֲדָשָׁה מֵאִתִּי תֵצֵא, חִדּוּשׁ תּוֹרָה מֵאִתִּי תֵצֵא. אָמַר רַבִּי בֶּרֶכְיָה בְּשֵׁם רַבִּי יִצְחָק אֲרִיסְטוֹן עָתִיד הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לַעֲשׂוֹת לַעֲבָדָיו הַצַּדִּיקִים לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא וְכָל מִי שֶׁלֹּא אָכַל נְבֵלוֹת בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה זוֹכֶה לִרְאוֹתוֹ לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, הֲדָא הוּא דִכְתִיב (ויקרא ז, כד): וְחֵלֶב נְבֵלָה וְחֵלֶב טְרֵפָה יֵעָשֶׂה לְכָל מְלָאכָה וְאָכֹל לֹא תֹאכְלֻהוּ, בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁתֹּאכְלוּ מִמֶּנּוּ לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא, לְפִיכָךְ משֶׁה מַזְהִיר לְיִשְׂרָאֵל וְאוֹמֵר לָהֶם (ויקרא יא, ב): זֹאת הַחַיָּה אֲשֶׁר תֹּאכֵלוּ.

Rabbi Yudan ben Rabbi Shimon said: The Behemoth and the Leviathan will engage in an animal fight before the righteous in the future. Anyone who was not a spectator at the animal fights of the nations of the world in this world, will merit to see it in the World to Come. How will they be slaughtered? The Behemoth will stab the Leviathan with its horns and tear it open, and the Leviathan will smash the Behemoth with its fins and stab it to death. The Sages say: Is this a valid ritual slaughter? But did we not learn: Everyone slaughters, and one may always slaughter, and one may slaughter with any item, except for the serrated side of the harvest sickle, a saw, the teeth of an animal, and a fingernail, because they strangle? Rabbi Avin bar Kahana said: The Holy One blessed be He said: “For [a new] Torah will emerge from Me” (Isaiah 51:4); a novel Torah ruling will emerge from Me. Rabbi Berekhya said in the name of Rabbi Yitzḥak: The Holy One blessed be He is destined to make a feast for His righteous servants in the future, and anyone who did not partake of unslaughtered carcasses in this world will be privileged to see it in the World to Come. That is what is written: “And the fat of an unslaughtered carcass and the fat of a mauled animal may be used for all labor; but you shall not eat it [ve’akhol lo tokheluhu]” (Leviticus 7:24). So that you will be able to partake of it in the future, therefore Moses cautions Israel and says to them: “These are the living beings that you may eat” (Leviticus 11:2).

This battle is also noted in the Midrash Tanchuma on Shemini 7:1:

וְהֵיכָן הֵן נִשְׁחָטִין. אֶלָּא זֶה לָזֶה מִזְדַּוְגִין שְׁנֵיהֶם, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: אֶחָד בָּאֶחָד יִגָּשׁוּ (איוב מא, ח). בְּהֵמוֹת יִגַּשׁ בַּלִּוְיָתָן וְאוֹחֵז בְּקַרְנָיו וּבוֹקֵעַ. וְלִוְיָתָן הֵפֶךְ יִהְיֶה מִיתָתוֹ, שֶׁמַּכֶּה אוֹתוֹ בִּזְנָבוֹ וְהוֹרְגוֹ, וְהַצַּדִּיקִים הוֹלְכִין וְנוֹטְלִין מָנוֹת מָנוֹת. מִכָּאן שְׁחִיטָה. אֶלָּא בִּשְׁבִיל לִבְדֹּק וּלְצָרֵף אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל

And [so] how are they slaughtered? Rather, they come and fight, one with the other, as stated (in Job 41:8), “One approaches to the other.” The behemoths approach the leviathan and hold him by his horn and split him, and the leviathan’s death [that he inflicts] will be the opposite, as he smites him with his tail and kills him. [Then] the righteous ones go and all take portions. From here [we see] that ritual slaughter was given only to examine and to purify (rt.: tsrp) Israel.

As far as a greater background, we can begin to answer your questions as to why we don't find it now...

First note the Gemara in Bava Basra 74b

וְאַף בְּהֵמוֹת בְּהַרְרֵי אֶלֶף – זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה בְּרָאָם, וְאִלְמָלֵי נִזְקָקִין זֶה לָזֶה מַחֲרִיבִין כָּל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ. מָה עָשָׂה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא? סֵירַס הַזָּכָר, וְצִינֵּן הַנְּקֵבָה וּשְׁמָרָהּ לַצַּדִּיקִים לֶעָתִיד לָבֹא, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״הִנֵּה נָא כֹחוֹ בְמׇתְנָיו״ – זֶה זָכָר, ״וְאוֹנוֹ בִּשְׁרִירֵי בִטְנוֹ״ – זוֹ נְקֵבָה.

And He created even the beasts on the thousand hills (see Psalms 50:10) male and female. And they were so enormous that if they would have coupled and produced offspring, they would have destroyed the entire world. What did the Holy One, Blessed be He, do? He castrated the male and cooled the sexual desire of the female and preserved it for the righteous in the future. As it is stated about the beasts: “Lo now, his strength is in his loins” (Job 40:16); this is referring to the male. The continuation of the verse: “And his force is in the stays of his body”; this is the female, alluding to the idea that they did not use their genitals for the purpose of procreation.

This idea is similarly expressed in Bereishis Rabbah 7:4

So it was created but it did not produce any kin and is clearly being "saved" until the right time.

As per the Pirkei DeRebbi Eliezer 11:4 it was created on the sixth day of creation and the midrash in Vayikra Rabbah 36:4 relates that it was created only due to the merit of Yaakov Avinu.

And the sheer size of it is noted in Vayikra Rabbah 22:10

בְּהֵמוֹת בְּהַרְרֵי אָלֶף, רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ וְרַבָּנָן, רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אוֹמֵר בְּהֵמָה אַחַת הִיא וּרְבוּצָה עַל אֶלֶף הָרִים וְאֶלֶף הָרִים מְגַדְּלִין לָהּ כָּל מִינֵי עֲשָׂבִים וְהִיא אוֹכֶלֶת, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (איוב מ, כ): כִּי בוּל הָרִים יִשְׂאוּ לוֹ. וְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אָמַר בְּהֵמָה אַחַת הִיא רְבוּצָה עַל אֶלֶף הָרִים וְאֶלֶף הָרִים מְגַדְּלִין לָהּ מַאֲכָל לַאֲכִילָתָן שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים, וְהִיא אוֹכֶלֶת, מַאי טַעְמָא (ישעיה סה, י): וְהָיָה הַשָּׁרוֹן לִנְוֵה צֹאן. וְרַבָּנָן אָמְרֵי בְּהֵמָה אַחַת הִיא וּרְבוּצָה עַל אֶלֶף הָרִים וְאֶלֶף הָרִים מְגַדְּלִין לָהּ מִינֵי בְּהֵמוֹת, וְהִיא אוֹכֶלֶת, מַאי טַעְמָא, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (איוב מ, כ): וְכָל חַיַּת הַשָּׂדֶה יְשַׂחֲקוּ שָׁם, וְאֶפְשָׁר כֵּן אִית בְּעִיר אָכֵיל בְּעִיר, אָמַר רַבִּי תַּנְחוּמָא גְּדוֹלִים הֵם מַעֲשֵׂה הָאֱלֹהִים מַה מְּשֻׁנִּין הֵם מַעֲשָׂיו שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, וּמֵהֵיכָן הוּא שׁוֹתֶה, רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ, רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר כָּל מַה שֶּׁהַיַּרְדֵּן מַכְנִיס אַחַת לְשִׁשָּׁה חֳדָשִׁים הוּא עוֹשֶׂה גְּמִיעָה אֶחָת, מַאי טַעְמָא, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (איוב מ, כג): הֵן יַעֲשֹׁק נָהָר וְלֹא יַחְפּוֹז. רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ אָמַר כָּל מַה שֶּׁהַיַּרְדֵּן מַכְנִיס לִשְׁנֵים עָשָׂר חֳדָשִׁים הוּא עוֹשֶׂה אוֹתוֹ גְּמִיעָה אַחַת, מַאי טַעְמָא (איוב מ, כג): יִבְטַח כִּי יָגִיחַ יַרְדֵּן אֶל פִּיהוּ, וְיֵשׁ בָּהֶם לִכְלוּךְ פֶּה, רַב הוּנָא בְּשֵׁם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אָמַר אֵין בָּהֶם לִכְלוּךְ פֶּה, וּמֵהֵיכָן הוּא שׁוֹתֶה, תָּנֵי רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחָאי נָהָר יוֹצֵא מֵעֵדֶן וּשְׁמוֹ יוּבַל וּמִשָּׁם הוּא שׁוֹתֶה, מַאי טַעְמָא, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (ירמיה יז, ח): וְעַל יוּבַל יְשַׁלַּח שָׁרָשָׁיו

“Animals on thousands of hills” (Psalms 50:10); Rabbi Yoḥanan, Reish Lakish, and the Rabbis, Rabbi Yoḥanan says: It is one animal that is lying on one thousand mountains, and one thousand mountains grow many varieties of grasses for it, and it eats, as it is stated: “For produce of mountains will be carried to it” (Job 40:20). Reish Lakish said: It is one animal lying on one thousand mountains, and one thousand mountains grow food for it, so it will be food for the righteous, and it eats. What is the source? “The Sharon will be a pasture for flocks” (Isaiah 65:10). The Rabbis say: It is one animal and it is lying on one thousand mountains, and one thousand mountains grow various types of animals for it, and it eats. What is the source? “All the beasts of the field will frolic there” (Job 40:20). Is that possible, that an animal [behema] eats an animal? Rabbi Tanḥuma said: God’s deeds are great, how extraordinary are the deeds of the Holy One blessed be He. From where does it drink? Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Everything that the Jordan takes in over the course of six months, it swallows in one gulp. What is the source? As it is stated: “Behold, it can swallow a river, it need not rush” (Job 40:23). Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: Everything that the Jordan takes in over the course of twelve months, it swallows in one gulp. What is the source? “It is secure, even if it draws the Jordan into its mouth” (Job 40:23). It has enough just to wet the mouth. Rav Huna said in the name of Rabbi Yosei: It is not even enough just to wet the mouth. From where, then, does it drink? Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai taught: A river emerges from Eden and its name is Yuval, and it drinks from there, as it is stated: “And it shall spread its roots alongside a stream [yuval]” (Jeremiah 17:8).

questions.title_en: Problem of tribal courts in case of litigants from different tribes
questions.question:
On Sanhedrin 16b we learn from the verse Devarim 16:18 that each city and tribe were required to set up a court of 23. The Ramban asks the question, why is it necessary to establish a tribal court if there is a court in every city? He suggests two anwers: either it is necessary when a city is divided between two tribes (see Sanhedrin 111b or Tosafot), or the tribes appointed a tribal supreme court for the difficult cases. But what happens if חו"ח there is an adultery or other forbidden relations, and the two individuals are from a different tribe?* Each should go to her/his own tribal court (see Rashi), which is ambiguous in this case.

* I suppose this rule only applies to capital cases and not monetary ones, and I can only think about arayot that involves more than one litigants. If you know other examples, please comment!

questions.title_en: How did they verify membership of seven Canaanite nations?
questions.question:
Following "defining-a-defensive-war", in Rambam Kings_and_Wars.5.5, we've established conditions for killing non-combatants:

"It is a positive commandment to annihilate the seven nations... Anyone who chances upon one of them and does not kill him violates a negative commandment... [However] The memory of them has already been obliterated.
Similarly, it is a positive commandment to destroy the [memory of] Amalek".

I imagine myself leaving Egypt, surviving 40 years in the wilderness, and joining Joshua in his legendary conquest of the land of Israel. As a part of a Legion, I enter a local house and meet a family with no visible national attributes.

As Rambam mentions, we do not currently possess a proper understanding of those nations' qualities, but in Biblical times, those were either evident or passed down through the tradition.

  • How were members of the 8 nations determined, including women and children? For example, did they not take foreign wives?
  • Was there a test (similar to יודעת איש), or was it based on Chazakah alone?
  • (Maybe unrelated) Should they be allowed to live out of Safek (doesn't "do not murder" still apply)?

A similar question would apply to Moses waging war on the Midianites (Num 31). In this case, they went out to another kingdom. How did they determine the borders of their kingdom and distinguish the natives from immigrants and tourists?

Another example is Saul's war against the Amalekites - I don't see the scripture mentioning any clear criteria for humans or animals, nor do I see any magic involved. How did they determine if a person is or is not an Amalekite?

questions.title_en: How could Korah know the number of parshiyos in the Torah?
questions.question: The answer here notes that when Korach argued with Moshe and Aharon, according to Midrash Tanchuma Korach 1, Korach mentioned that the number of parshiyos in the Torah is 275. How could he know this number, if the Torah itself had not yet been written?

answers.text:
Potential answers:

  1. He didn't and a later rabbi is fleshing out the dispute.
  2. He was on such a holy spiritual plane that he intuited that there were 275 parshiot.
  3. 275 is the gematria for evil and Korach really said the Torah was bad. A later rabbi bowdlerized his complaint.
  4. He learned it in a prophecy when everyone temporarily became a prophet at Har Sinai.
  5. A angel or demon told him.

questions.title_en: Why does the Mishnah specify that the poor person obligated to recline Pesach night is Jewish?
questions.question:
The Mishnah in Pesachim (10:1) obligates even a Jewish poor person in reclining:

וַאֲפִלּוּ עָנִי שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא יֹאכַל עַד שֶׁיָּסֵב

Even the poorest of Jews should not eat the meal on Passover night until he reclines on his left side, as free and wealthy people recline when they eat

Why does the Mishnah need to specify that the indigent person is Jewish? Isn't it obvious that a non-Jew isn't obligated in the passover rituals?

(Not my question. Heard it recently and haven't seen it addressed)

answers.text:
The issue was originally raised in the Tosafos Rabbi Akiva Eiger on Pesachim 1:10, who suggested removing שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל.

בתוי"ט ד"ה ואפילו עני. עד שתחשך. ובספר ברית שלום על התורה כ' (בפרשת בא) בשם החכם מוה' יעקב זצ"ל דיש לפרש לפי מה דאי' ריש ברכות משעה שעני נכנס לאכול פתו. ופירש"י עני שאין לו נר אוכל מבע"י. ולזה קאמר הכא דאפילו עני שבישראל שאין לו לקנות נר ובכל השנה אוכל מבע"י אפ"ה בליל פסח לא יאכל עד שתחשך:

Tosafos Yom Tov, heading and even a poor person. Until it gets dark. And in the sefer Bris Shalom on the Torah in the name of Moreh Horaah Yaakov זצ"ל, it is possible to explain according to what's brought in Brachos 2b Rabbi Ḥanina says that the time for the recitation of the evening Shema begins when the poor person enters to eat his bread (with salt). Rashi explains (this comment is missing in our gemara) *a poor person, who does not have a candle, eats while it's still daytime. Regading such a person it is stated here that even poor Jewish people who cannot purchase a candle during the year and eat while it's still daytime, even so, on the night of Pesach he should not start eating until it gets dark.

The heading in Tosafos Yom Tov includes שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל as one can check here: ואפילו עני כו'.

The commentary on gemara יפה עינים by R. Aryeh Leib Yellin from Bielsk Podlaski, Poland, rejects the modification of R. Akiva Eiger. On Pesachim 99b, R. Yellin states:

אפי' עני שבישראל. שמ"ר פ"כ מבאן כו' אפי' עני כו' עד שיסב שכבר עשה להם הקב"ה שנא' ויסב אלהים ומזה ראיה דלא כמ"ש הגרע"א בשם ס' ברית שלום לפרש דהאי אפי' עני כו'מוסב על למעלה דלא יאכל עד שתחשך אפי' עני שדרכו לאכול קודם צה"כ דמהמדרש מוכח אלמטה קאי כמש"ש מכאן אמרו רבותינו אפי' עני כו' וכפרש"י והרשב"ם:

Even the poor Jewish person. Midrash Shemos Rabba 20:18 has a drasha on the verse Shemos 13:18 on words וַיַּסֵּ֨ב אֱלֹהִ֧ים ׀ אֶת־הָעָ֛ם כו - so G-d led the people round about, etc:

מִכָּאן אָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ אֲפִלּוּ עָנִי שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא יֹאכַל עַד שֶׁיֵּסֵב, שֶׁכָּךְ עָשָׂה לָהֶם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: וַיַּסֵּב אֱלֹהִים.

from here our Rabbis said: “Even the poor of Israel may not eat until he reclines [yasev]” (Mishna Pesaḥim 10:1) as that is what the Holy One blessed be He did to them, as it is stated: “G-d led [the people] around [vayasev].”

From this (midrash) we have a proof that (the girsa in the mishna) is not like suggested by the G"R Akiva Eiger in the name of Sefer Bris Shalom which explains that the words "even a poor etc." refers to the above that he should not start eating until it gets dark, even the poor who usually eats before tzeis hakokhavim (3 average stars). Because the midrash proves about (using the word שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל) above as it states "from here our Rabbis said: Even the poor, etc." and like the comment Rashi on Chumash and Rashbam on Pesachim 99b

The point of R. Yellin is that the halakha of הסיבה - reclining or leaning to the left at the table is derived from the drasha in Shemos Rabba 20:18, and has to mirror its language. In turn, the reason why the midrash uses the word שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, is because it comments on the verse that uses the word הָעָ֛ם - the nation (with definite article the), which refers to the nation of Israel.

On a personal note, on many occasions I heard the explanation that eating with leaning at the seder represented דרך חרות - way of freedom, which meant that in the olden days free people used to lean while eating. I have never understood this idea, because sitting and leaning to the side regularly can damage one's spine.

However, the deep point of R' Yellin about sitting with derekh cheirus at the seder is different. At the seder,

חַיָּב אָדָם לִרְאוֹת אֶת־עַצְמוֹ כְּאִלּוּ הוּא יָצָא מִמִּצְרַיִם

each person must see himself as if he himself had come out of Egypt.

As the map below suggests, leaving Egypt, going east towards Sinai and leaning to the left means leaning towards Eretz Israel - the eventual destination, from which we are supposed to draw our sustenance. Hence we do so at the seder.

questions.title_en: Distinctive cultural traits of ancient Israelites in the Tanakh
questions.question:
The following description of the Israelites during the Egypt Exile appears numerous times in the Midrash (Sefaria Midrash):

"וְלֹא שִׁנּוּ אֶת שְׁמָם, וְלֹא שִׁנּוּ אֶת לְשׁוֹנָם"
"[the Israelites in Egypt] didn't change their language and clothes"

Maintaining cultural distinction was always important for the Jewish nation, as it says (Lev 20:23): "Do not follow the statutes of the nation [that I am driving out before you]," or (Lev 18:3): "Do not follow their statutes", and so rules Rambam in MT Foreign_Worship and Customs of the Nations.

However, all I can find in the Tanakh is the divine demand for differences only in cultic/religious practices, but no positive examples of native Biblical Jewish culture, such as language (i.e., the Torah doesn't demand to speak a specific language), clothes, cuisine, architecture, tools, furniture, houseware, personal names, music, dances, national symbols (the Star of David), and more.

That leads me to the questions:

  • Are there descriptions of distinctive cultural traits of the ancient Hebrews/Israelites/Judeans in the Tanakh or 2nd-Temple literature that I miss?
  • If not, why doesn't the Torah establish distinctively Jewish cultural traits?

answers.text: Rav Moshe Feinstein (Igros Moshe OC vol. 4 nu.66) argued that it could be that these rules only applied before the giving of the Torah. After that, following the Torah is enough.

questions.title_en: Do both adulterers require separate treatment?
questions.question:
If a man commits adultery with a married woman—committing adultery with another man’s wife—the adulterer and the adulteress shall be put to death. (Lev 20.10)

  • Do both adulterers require separate warnings?
  • Do both adulterers require separate [pairs of] witnesses?
  • Do both adulterers require separate trials?
  • What happens if one witness is Pasul as a relative of one partner?
  • Can one be ruled to be exempt, but the other executed (for consensual cases)?

"וְהָיָ֣ה כְשִׁבְתּ֔וֹ עַ֖ל כִּסֵּ֣א מַמְלַכְתּ֑וֹ וְכָ֨תַב ל֜וֹ אֶת־מִשְׁנֵ֨ה הַתּוֹרָ֤ה הַזֹּאת֙ עַל־סֵ֔פֶר מִלִּפְנֵ֥י הַכֹּהֲנִ֖ים הַלְוִיִּֽם׃" (Deut 17.18)
"וַיְהִי כְּכַלּוֹת מֹשֶׁה לִכְתֹּב אֶת־דִּבְרֵי הַתּוֹרָה־הַזֹּאת עַל־סֵפֶר עַד תֻּמָּם׃" (Deut 31.24)
"וַיִּדֹּ֨ם הַשֶּׁ֜מֶשׁ וְיָרֵ֣חַ עָמָ֗ד עַד־יִקֹּ֥ם גּוֹי֙ אֹֽיְבָ֔יו הֲלֹא־הִ֥יא כְתוּבָ֖ה עַל־סֵ֣פֶר הַיָּשָׁ֑ר" (Josh 10.13)
"וַיֵּלְכ֤וּ הָֽאֲנָשִׁים֙ וַיַּעַבְר֣וּ בָאָ֔רֶץ וַיִּכְתְּב֧וּהָ לֶֽעָרִ֛ים לְשִׁבְעָ֥ה חֲלָקִ֖ים עַל־סֵ֑פֶר" (Josh 18.9)

"וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יי אֶל־מֹשֶׁ֗ה כְּתֹ֨ב זֹ֤את זִכָּרוֹן֙ בַּסֵּ֔פֶר" (Ex 17.14)
"וְ֠כָתַב אֶת־הָאָלֹ֥ת הָאֵ֛לֶּה הַכֹּהֵ֖ן בַּסֵּ֑פֶר וּמָחָ֖ה אֶל־מֵ֥י הַמָּרִֽים" (Num 5.23)
"וַיִּכְתֹּ֤ב יְהוֹשֻׁ֨עַ֙ אֶת־הַדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֔לֶּה בְּסֵ֖פֶר" (Josh 24.26)

What is the difference between the use of the two prepositions - when something is written על הספר and when בספר?

answers.text:
Malbim Beur Hamilot on Yirmiyahu 8:8 writes (with clarifications from Sefer haCarmel, כתב, p. 433, and also ספר, סופר, p. 596):

יש הבדל בין כותב ובין סופר, הכותב יהיה על כל דבר, וכתבתם על מזוזת, כתבם על לוח, וכתבת על האבנים והסופר כותב בספרים, ולא תמצא שם תואר כותב בשום מקום :

There is a difference between writing and inscribing. Person writing (כותב) is doing so upon any matter (requiring על): writes upon (על) mezuzah (Devarim 6:9, 11:20), upon (על) a board, upon (על) stones (Devarim 27:8) (in these cases the focus is on material of writing or the product created by writing).

The person inscribing is perfoming in (-ב) books. (In these cases the focus is on the process of writing).

We do not find the adjective כותב describing the writer in any place in scripture, (but סופר).

questions.title_en: Are blessings and curses something other than prophecy or prayer?
questions.question:
It seems that blessings/curses can either be prophecies regarding the future or positive/negative prayers regarding someone else's future.

However, in Tanach (e.g., those of Yitzchak, Bilam & Birchas Kohanim) it seems that they are something else, quite apart from prophecy or prayer.

Is there another option for defining what curses and blessings are and how they work? Are they somehow causal? If so, how are they different than prayer which isn't as sure a bet? Are they meant to influence a person psychologically?

questions.title_en: Does a Jewish man who did not have Bar Mitzva count for a minyan?
questions.question: I'm a Jewish man and I chose not to have a bar mitzva ceremony. Occasionally, I get asked to participate in a minyan. Would I even halachically count?

answers.text:
There is no such thing as a bar mitzvah ceremony that confers adulthood on you.

If you are halachically Jewish, male, and have had your 13th Hebrew birthday you are an adult and can be counted for a minyan.

questions.title_en: Is it allowed to add ketchup to a plate of cholent on Shabbos (klei sheini)?
questions.question:
Is it allowed to add ketchup to your plate of Cholent on Shabbos, where that plate is considered a kli sheini?

Do we assume the ketchup is getting cooked?

answers.text: Rav Moshe Feinstein writes in Igros Moshe O.C.4 74:5 (bottom of left column) that you may pour ketchup on hot meat in a kli sheini, because in order to forbid it you would need 2 chumrahs: בִּשּׁוּל אֲחַר בִּשּׁוּל בִּדְבַר לַח, and that a דָבָר גּוּשׁ is treated like a kli rishon.

questions.title_en: How did Rabbi Eliezer cause Rabban Gamliel to die by saying Tachanun?
questions.question:
The Gemara (B"M 59b) says that Rabbi Eliezer said Tachanun and Rabban Gamliel died as a result. Hashem allots a certain number of years to each person.

How can someone’s prayer shorten someone else’s lifespan?

answers.text:
I love this story. Most, if not ALL, scholars misunderstand it, focusing on "Not in heaven" as the Talmudic Asmachta for breaking out of existing tradition.

In reality, the whole story is about the respect one should pay to the sages and the heavy price one pays for disrespecting them.

To take the story of Akhnai in the proper context, one should start with a list of sayings that precede it on 59a:

"Rav Hisda says: All the gates of Heaven are apt to be locked, except for the gates of prayer for victims of verbal mistreatment"
"Rabbi Abbahu says: There are three sins before whose transgressors the curtain [hapargod] between the world and the Divine Presence is not locked; their sins reach the Divine Presence. They are: Verbal mistreatment, robbery, and idol worship..." "And Rabbi Ḥelbo says: A person must always be careful about sustaining the honor of his wife, as a blessing is found in a person’s house only because of his wife."

And check out the statement that immediately follows the story:

" The Sages taught: One who verbally mistreats the convert violates three prohibitions."

TLDR: As you can see, our story is set within the discussion of "verbal mistreatment"; therefore, we can conclude that R"G's indirect insult of R"E through the Herem and his resulting death demonstrate the severity of the disgrace of Talmidey Chachamim.

Explanation:

In Rosh Hashana Mishna 2.9, we encounter R"G's [somewhat undemocratic] attempt to establish his political authority over more prominent sages (R"Y here). As the Gemmora explicates, that move was mandated, as the survival of the sages and the tradition depended on cooperation and adaptation to the Roman rulership. E.g., it says that the sages can't fix the new year until the Nassi coordinates it with the Roman authorities in Syria.

Our story is the continuation and escalation of the aforementioned affair. R"Y clearly acted under the command of R"G to force R"E to comply with R"G's authority and let the latter install practices not supported by the existing tradition. To remind you that R"E was the only sage who was mentioned as "*one who never says things he didn't hear from his rabbis", so he was the one who insisted on sticking to the tradition.

Here are some textual clues to prove my point:

  • R"E won all reasonable arguments
  • Nobody claimed the existence of an alternative tradition
  • There was NO voting, and "follow the majority" was NOT mentioned in this clash
  • The divine voice was proven authoritative in the argument of B"H and B"S (Eruvin 13b): "a Divine Voice emerged and proclaimed: Both these and those are the words of the living God. However, the halakha follows the opinion of Beit Hillel." Therefore, "Not following divine voice" could NOT be an existing practice.
  • The divine voice did NOT rule a single case, but claimed that R"E's traditional opinion should be followed EVERYWHERE!
  • To prove his point, R"Y stood on his feet. This is the sign of authority, not intellect. He personified R"G's will as the Nasi.
  • R"Y claimed, "Not in Heaven". What is it? If it were an existing principle, it would be explained by reference to earlier rabbis. However, in the text, it is apologized for by a later Tanna/Amora, R' Yeremiya. Another evidence that the principle was conceived "on the spot".
  • As the Gemmora continues, the court was not satisfied with the intellectual discussion, but continues to humiliate R"E: "the Sages brought all the ritually pure items deemed pure by the ruling of Rabbi Eliezer concerning the oven and burned them in fire" - was that really necessary?
  • Furthermore, "... the Sages reached a consensus in his regard and ostracized him". Why? Was it a Halachic or a political move? Let's see God's reaction: "[R"E's] eyes shed tears, and as a result the entire world was afflicted: One-third of its olives were afflicted, and one-third of its wheat, and one-third of its barley. And some say that even dough kneaded in a woman’s hands spoiled. The Sages taught: There was great anger on that day, as any place that Rabbi Eliezer fixed his gaze was burned."
  • Why would there be divine anger if the sages were motivated purely by the desire to fulfill God's will?
  • Wait, wasn't God pleased by the fight? Isn't He quoted saying, "My children have triumphed over Me"? Let's see who says that. It was brought, again, in the name of a later Tanna, R' Nathan. As one can notice, that later insertion does not fit the divine rage. Clearly, that was an attempt to harmonize the harsh event.
  • R"G knew exactly why God was angry with him when he experienced a storm. He rightfully admitted his involvement in the affair and claimed that it wasn't for his personal gain, but the necessity to revive Judaism. He wished to utilize his political authority to minimize Rabbinic disagreements, even at the price of breaking the tradition.
  • Since the sea calmed down, we could infer that the heavens agreed with his approach. So why did he die at the end? I suggest, [probably in his briefing with R"Y and going as far as banning R"E], that he crossed the line of mistreating a great sage. As I mentioned above, he was already warned in the story "Is Maariv mandatory?". But he didn't listen.
  • The story ends with R"E described as being in great pain and suffering enormous humiliation. So, since the Gemmora has already established that "the gates of mistreatment are never shut", once R"E had an opportunity to pour his soul before Heaven, his distress outweighed R"G's honor and the latter was "executed".

So the moral of this story is simple - if you disrespect and disgrace a renowned sage, God takes it very personally.

questions.title_en: Re-using the tune from a song about Avoda Zara
questions.question:
I heard in a shiur a cute story about someone who made a tikkun for a neshama, by singing one of his tunes during hakafot. The story was about taking a tune and making it holy, and how this is a positive. It made me think of this question.

So, unrelated to said positive, I want to ask if we are generally allowed to take a tune from a song about Avoda Zara - just the melody, not the lyrics - and make it into a song about something holy?

We are strictly forbidden to get hana'ah (pleasure or benefit) from Avoda Zara, even indirectly, but the melody is abstract. Maybe it is similar to benefiting from a mountain that was worshiped?

הגוים העובדים את ההרים ואת הגבעות, הן מתרין

With regard to the halakha in the case of the gentiles who worship the mountains and the hills, the mountains and hills are permitted [but what is upon them is forbidden] (Mishna Avoda Zara 3:5)

answers.text:
There's a great article on Contrafaction in Jewish prayer by Joshua Jacobson. Pulling out some of the relevant halachic opinions from it, because it is rather lengthy!

Opinions against:

Rabbi Yehudah He-Hasid (c. 1150 - 1217) wrote, “In the case of a hymn composed by a priest for worship in a non-Jewish service, even if a Jew considers it to be a beautiful form of praise, he should not chant it to God in Hebrew.”

Rabbi Yehudah Al-Harizi (c. 1170-1235) wrote of his visit to a Baghdad synagogue in 1220: “The cantors don’t understand the words, and the people have no idea what they are saying. And instead of the holy (k’doshim) songs of [King] David, they sing the songs of prostitutes (k’deishim).”

In the Shulhan arukh, Rabbi Joseph Caro (1488-1575) wrote, “If a sh’liah tsibbur sings using gentile melodies, you should protest that he should not do such a thing. And if he doesn’t listen, you should remove him.”

The Italian Rabbi Samuel ben Elhanan Archivolti (1515-1611) wrote, “What can we say? How can we justify the actions of a few hazzanim of our day, who chant the holy prayers to the tunes of popular secular songs? While reading sacred texts they are thinking of obscenities and lewd things.”

In 1605 Rabbi Ben Zion Sarfati (d. 1610) wrote that in his youth in the synagogue of Padua, Italy, his choir “used to sing the whole order of K’dushah at the request of [Rabbi Meir]. Certainly it was not worse, indeed better than the those who raised their voices against us, singing [the K’dushah to the tunes of] the vulgar songs that are sung outdoors in the streets.”

In his Shirei y’hudah published in Amsterdam in 1696, Rabbi Y’hudah Leib Zelichower (d. 1709) wrote, But now, in this generation… they know not, they do not understand, they walk in darkness, they abandon the ancient melodies and toss them behind their backs, they laugh and make fun of them saying, “that’s old stuﬀ, and we get no pleasure from them,” and they fabricate new melodies to take their place, either [melodies] of their own, or they borrow them from their theaters and bring them into God’s Temple, and they sound like the melodies that go with mixed dancing. And there are even some of them who learn melodies from the uncircumcised… and sing them in our synagogues. Have you ever heard of such evil? Could God desire this kind of song and music?

In an anonymous pamphlet entitled Tokhehah m’gulah (Open Demands), written in Styria (now Austria) in the seventeenth century, we find several complaints lodged against hazzanim, including, “If you become used to foreign melodies, you will manage to destroy the proper kavvanah. And the listeners are focused on the melodies to such an extent that even Torah scholars haven’t a clue how to concentrate and achieve kavvanah. What happens is that people become used to going to the synagogue [merely] to listen to pleasant singing.”

Moshe Vital, a well-known Sephardic cantor in Jerusalem in the early twentieth century wrote, “For artistic and theological reasons a Sephardic cantor is forbidden to introduce secular songs into the synagogue… Sometimes one of our cantors works also as a secular singer who entertains others with secular songs, and it is quite common to hear from his mouth the melody of a love song merged with sections of prayers, such as a Kaddish or a K’dushah… But he should allow himself to do this only if the melody is not recognizable to the congregation.”

Opinions for:

Yet not all opinions have been against contrafaction. Some rabbis entertained a more positive view. Some expressed the hope that using melodies that people already knew and loved would encourage greater participation in the worship service. Others subscribed to the Kabbalistic idea that there is a spark of holiness in even the most degraded objects, and that it is a great mitzvah to rescue these sparks and redeem them into the service of the Holy One.

In the sixteenth century, Rabbi Israel Najara (c. 1555–c. 1625) wrote He- brew sacred lyrics to be sung to melodies of then-popular Arab and Turkish songs. His intention was to distract young people from the secular world, allowing them to sing their favorite tunes, but with new, uplifting lyrics. “The mouths of liars and the singing of sensual songs will be blocked, and they will no longer think about love songs when they see [my] songs.”

Mizrahi (Eastern) Jews, in particular Syrians, continue the practice of contrafaction in their pizmonim. The Syrian payy’tan Raphael Isaac Antibi defended this practice, citing the Kabbalistic interpretation. A melody is a holy spark. When you play love songs the spark is hidden in its shell. Therefore in every new melody that the gentiles compose you must establish words from the scribes, words of holiness, in order to extract the spark from the “other side” [i.e. Satan] to the side of holiness. And this is an obligation no less than preventing sinners from sinning, causing many people to turn from sin, to extract that which is precious from that which is evil, to choose the sparks of holiness.

Rabbi Israel Moshe Hazzan (1808-1862), who served in Jerusalem’s High Religious Court, defended the practice of borrowing a beautiful melody that had been used in non-Jewish worship. And I testify by heaven and earth that when I was in Smyrna, the great city of scholars and mystics, I saw some of the outstanding religious authorities who were also great creators of the science of music, headed by the wonderful Rabbi Abraham Ha-Kohein Ariash of blessed memory, who secretly used to go (behind the screen) of the Christian church on their holy days to learn the special melodies from them and to adapt them to the High Holiday prayers which require great humility. And from those same melodies they would arrange the most remarkable blessings and holy prayers, and it is clear from this that the tune is not of the essence, but the sacred words.

Jacob S. Kassin (1900-1994), Chief Rabbi of the Syrian Community of New York, echoed this sentiment. [Borrowing melodies and providing them with new, sacred Hebrew texts is done for a] good reason, a reason of fundamental importance, and it is correct that it is said about it “that it is good.” This is so because the melody is a holy spark. Because when one plays sensual love songs, the spark is submerged in the k’lippot [waste coverings]. It is for this reason that it is necessary to establish a foundation of holy words—drawn from the mouths of scholars and from the mouths of books—for any tune with a non-Jewish source, in order to lead the spark from the realm of evil to the realm of holiness. This is an obligation in the same way that it is an obligation to draw sinners to good, to turn away from iniquity, and to bring out the precious from the vile. It is an obligation to make clear the holy sparks. So it is with holy songs. The holy sparks bring light to the just.

Those who say that it is assur to use a tune that is used for avodah zara:

The Magen Avraham Orach Chaim Siman 53:31 quoting the Sefer Chasidim Siman 238 says any melody that is played in front of idolatry should not be used as a melody for Hashem. Mishneh Berurah in Chaim Siman 53:82 quoting the Bach Siman 127 says that the issur applies only to those specific melodies that are uniquely designated for avodah zara. Kaf Hachaim in Orach Chaim Siman 53:115 quotes all the above sources as well. Shu"t Yabia Omer Orach Chaim 6:7 in the first few paragraphs implies that it's assur.

See חבל נחלתו ט:ה for a full discussion with many sources.

Bach (responsum 127) forbids repurposing a tune that is uniquely associated with idolatry. On the other hand, if it is merely used in an idolatrous ritual, without being identified with idolatry, he permits it:

[השמטה: מה שמזמרי' בבתי כנסיות בניגוני' שמזמרי' בהם בבית תפלתם. נראה שאין אוסר אלא דווקא באותן ניגונים שהם מיוחדי' להעכ"ם מאחר שהוא חוק לע"ז כמו מצבה שאסורה בכל מקום מפני שעשאוה כנעני' חוק לע"ז. ואין ראי' להתיר גם את זה מהא דתנן בפ' ד' מיתות מצות הנהרגי' היו מתיזי' כו' ע"ש ובגמר' תנינא א"ל ר' יהודא לחכמים אף אני יודע שמיתה מנוולת היא ע"ש וא"כ איכא למימר ה"נ בניגוני' דלאו מינייהו קא גמרי אלא ע"י חכמת המוסקי' דאין לומר להחמיר כר' יודא דלית ליה סברא זו דהא כבר פסקו הפוסקים הלכה כרבנן מ"מ נראה דאין ראי' מכאן לפי מ"ש התוספות וז"ל תימא דמשמע הכא דאע"ג דחוקה היא כיון דכתיב ק' כו' ע"ש אלמא דאפילו כתוב באורייתא לא מהני כשנעשה חוק לע"ז. כ"ש באותן ניגוני' אבל אם אינם מיוחדי' נראה דאין בזה איסור דבהא ודאי איכא למימר דלא מינייהו גמרינן:]

Omission: regarding what is sung in synagogues using the melodies that are sung in their (non-Jewish) house of worship. It appears that the prohibition applies only to those specific melodies that are uniquely designated for the gentiles, since this constitutes a ḥoq (a fixed custom or statute) of idolatry—just as a matzevah (sacred pillar) is forbidden everywhere, because the Canaanites established it as an idolatrous practice. And there is no proof to permit even these melodies from the case taught in the chapter "Four Types of Capital Punishment" [Sanhedrin], regarding the execution method of beheading, where the Mishnah states: “The prescribed method for those executed by the sword was decapitation,” etc. And in the Gemara, Rabbi Yehuda says to the Sages, “I too know that it is a degrading death,” etc. Thus, one could argue similarly here: that in the case of the melodies, we are not learning from the gentiles themselves, but rather through the musical knowledge of experts. And one should not claim that we must be stringent in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda’s position, for his reasoning was not accepted—since the halakhic authorities have already ruled that the law follows the Sages. Nonetheless, there is no proof from that case (of execution) to our issue, in light of what Tosafot writes, and I quote: “It is difficult, for it seems from here that even though it is a ḥoq, since it is written in the Torah…” etc. (see there). From this it emerges that even if something is written in the Torah, it does not help if it has already become an idolatrous custom. All the more so, then, regarding those melodies that are uniquely identified with idolatrous worship. However, if the melodies are not uniquely associated [with idolatry], then it would seem there is no prohibition. For in that case, one can certainly say that we are not deriving from them (the gentiles).

questions.title_en: Sheva mayos vishivim (770), mi yodeya?
questions.question:
B"H

What are some significances of the number 770 in the Torah and Judaism? Gematrias are allowed if they are relevant to a specific topic.

answers.text:
Gematria of the word קערת is 770. It is significant in Midrash Bamidbar Rabba 14:12 describing the offering of Nachshon ben Aminadav:

Rabbi Shemaya said: From where do you say that it is regarding Adam the first man that kaarat kesef (קערת כסף) is stated? It is because the tally of the years of Adam the first man was nine hundred and thirty years, and the numerical value of kaarat kesef is nine hundred and thirty.

The full calculation here is

  • Kof – 100; ayin – 70; resh – 200; tav – 400; together they sum to 770.
  • Kaf – 20; samekh – 60; peh – 80; together they sum to 160.

The two sums together equal 930 (we do not have a question about 930 on Mi Yodeya).

Alternatively, several words from Tanakh have gematria 770.

  • The well named עין-שמש - Ein Shemesh (Eye of the sun) on the border between Binyamin and Yehudah, Yehoshua 15:7 or Yehoshua 18:17.
  • משכית - image, figure; imagination, conceit, Vayikra 26:1, Bamidbar 33:52, Yechezkel 8:12, Tehilim 73:7, Mishlei 18:11, Mishlei 25:11.
  • עשת - bar of metal, tablet (of ivory) Shir haShirim 5:14; steel (in modern Hebrew).

בית משיח — “Beit Moshiach / the House of Moshiach”

בית: ב(2)+י(10)+ת(400)=412

משיח: מ(40)+ש(300)+י(10)+ח(8)=358

412+358=770

Used homiletically for the dwelling/manifestation of the Davidic redemption.

B"H

770 E. Parkway is the address of the Chabad headquarters of America, which also has the gematria of בית משיח and פרצת, and is the place that the future Messiah will first be revealed at, according to the words of the Lubavitcher Rebbe. (Kuntress Beis Rabbenui Shebebbavel).

It's significant because that's the location where the Moshiach is waiting to redeem Yisroel, in the house of our Rebbe in Babylon.

ולהעיר, ש"בית משיח" בגימטריא "פרצת" (770). ודו"ק

questions.question: If I damaged private school or camp property years ago (as a halachic adult), am I now obligated to reach out and offer to repay? Are there any specific factors that would affect the halacha?

questions.title_en: Drinking less than the shiur for a Bracha Achrona
questions.question:
The Mishna Brura in 210:1 cites a dispute as to whether one makes a Bracha Achrona on a drink only after drinking a Reviis within כדי אכילת פרס.

If one would like to sip on a drink, it permissible to intentionally drink it slower and then simply not make a Bracha Achrona, or must one save a Reviis to drink quickly at the end?

questions.title_en: Halacha of eating two foods with the same bracha overlapping with each other
questions.question:
If one is snacking and drinking a beverage not during a meal, and they finish with the food and do not anticipate finishing the beverage until much later, what is the procedure regarding afterblessings if both are the same bracha?

Should they:

  1. Say a bracha achrona on the first food and then a new bracha rishona to continue drinking
  2. Say a bracha achrona on the first food and still bank on the original bracha rishona to continue drinking
  3. Wait until they're done drinking to say the bracha achrona for it all

questions.title_en: Can a Jew wear a linen shirt with a wool tallis?
questions.question: Is it allowed for Jews to wear a linen shirt when one is wearing a wool tallis, for example during Shacharit or when one is leading a service? Does just layering or contact constitute shatnez or does it require weaving or sewing?

answers.text: Yes it is allowed. The prohibition of shatnez applies when the two materials are combine via combing, spinning, sewing, etc. does not apply to different garments layered on one another

questions.title_en: Not believing in G-d - Jews in the Desert
questions.question:
I am a little bit confused on how to understand the disbelief of the Jews in the desert, and it is somewhat difficult to phrase my question.

How is it possible to not believe in G-d when the Jews saw all these many miracles in Egypt: the giving of the Torah, the filling of the Mishkan with G-d's Shekhina etc.?

Trying to answer my question, I could say that they might have believed that the miracles were done by Moshe, Aaron and Miriam. They could not see beyond! However, I would accept that once but not so many times. This rebelliousness prevailed all along.

How come then it is so "easy" to believe in G-d today, when we no longer witness unnatural miracles but back then, when people saw all these miracles and signs and so on, derailed so easily

answers.text:
A very thoughtful question! The Midrashim go at length to explain how the overwhelming majority of Jews did not participate in the sin of the Golden Calf, and the ones that did still believed in God, they just thought that they needed an intermediary in order to receive His blessings and guidance. Even the Eruv Rav - the Egyptian converts who started the whole matter, believed in God, but they also believed in other gods too.

The Midrashim, as usual, base on this on a close reading of the verses, rather than mere apologetics, and in this case, it's very easy to see when you know where to look. In order to see this methodically laid out, I recommend this shiur by Rabbi Dovid Gottleib. I will also share a Drasha that I wrote, based on it, for Parashat Ki Tisa, especially because it also deals with Bitachon, one of your tags:

There are two ways to hide a diamond. One is to hide it, and one is to bury it among  mundane items, like toy diamonds. In the case of the Chet HaEgel, the general flow of the story seems like the Jewish people bowed down to an idol, right after Har Sinai, and everyone focuses on that. However, the truth of the story is that only a few actually bowed down to the idol, a tiny tiny minority, probably just the Eruv Rav, and the rest of the 3 million Jewish people were doing something else…, and if we look closely at the pasukim, we can see it, without needing to look at Drash, Remez or Kabbalah.

Look at the language carefully: “The people saw that Moshe delayed in descending the mountain, and they gathered around Aaron and said, ‘Rise up, make for us gods that will go before us, because this man Moshe who brought us up from Egypt—we don’t know what happened to him.’” (Shemot 32:1). The problem begins not with a desire to abandon Hashem, but with confusion and fear over Moshe’s absence. They weren’t looking for a new god—they were looking for guidance, for something tangible to take Moshe’s place.

Even more striking is Aaron’s response. After making the calf, the people say, “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up from the land of Egypt.” (32:4). But Aaron immediately declares, “Tomorrow will be a festival for Hashem.” (32:5). If this was outright idol worship, why would Aaron sanctify it in Hashem's name? Clearly, the calf was never meant to replace Hashem for the vast majority of the 3 million Jews (as only 10,000 total ended up dying afterwards)—it was meant to replace Moshe to connect them to Hashem.

So, everyone thinks that the main message of Ki Tisa is how bad the Jews were, but that’s not true. The real message is the ending of the story. Hashem said to Moshe וְשָׁלַחְתִּי לְפָנֶיךָ מַלְאָךְ … and when Moshe told Benei Yisrael this, וַיִּשְׁמַע הָעָם אֶת־הַדָּבָר הָרָע הַזֶּה וַיִּתְאַבָּלוּ וְלֹא־שָׁתוּ אִישׁ עֶדְיוֹ עָלָיו. Moshe said to Hashem אִם־אֵין פָּנֶיךָ הֹלְכִים אַל־תַּעֲלֵנוּ מִזֶּה, and then וַיֹּאמֶר ה' אֶל־מֹשֶׁה גַּם אֶת־הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה אֲשֶׁר־דִּבַּרְתָּ אֶעֱשֶׂה כִּי־מָצָאתָ חֵן בְּעֵינַי וָאֵדָעֲךָ בְשֵׁם.

So, what was the sin? The sin was a sin of Bitachon. This one sin is something even the greatest of the greats failed in – such as Yaakov preparing gifts for Esav and bowing to him. It came from a place of humility – we felt we didn’t deserve Hashem. Hashem held that against us – nobody wants a friend, or a spouse, who is constantly feeling unworthy, not believing your promises to love them and look after them!

So let’s discuss some halachot about Bitachon for the remainder of the Dvar Torah, to help us do teshuva for the Chet Ha’egel and bring Moshiach!

People are very confused about Bitachon. There’s always an argument – someone says “just trust in Hashem” and someone retorts “but you have to make a hishtadlut!”, and the first person says “but it’s a mitzva to put our trust in Hashem, don’t you know the story of the man who sold his donkey and became a millionaire?” and the other person says “don’t YOU know the story of the person who’s child was sick, and he didn’t take them to the doctor and they died!”.

This is actually a battle between someone whose soul is rooted in Chesed, vs someone whose soul is rooted in Gevura. What is the answer to this puzzle? Well, it’s actually quite simple – we have a mitzva to make hishtadlut, but we are also commanded to realise that we are only doing that hishatdlut because Hashem commanded us to, not because we believe that hishtadlut has any power on its own. It doesn’t – we have to keep in mind that the blessing and success comes only from Hashem. This is why the Tzemach Tzeddek in Derech Mitzvotecha says that when it comes to hishtadlut, we are not allowed to make even one extra drop of effort more than required. If we need £5000 to get through the month, we must calculate exactly how much effort it takes to earn that, and then do that effort and no more.

So, why does Hashem want us to make effort? There are many reasons for this, but to cut to the chase, His blessings for us are so lofty, that they mamash do not fit into nature. They descend from the highest of heavens down to the level of Gan Eden, but to make the leap to the physical world, they need a vessel to be made by our own efforts. If they were to come any other way, the miracles would disrupt Hashem’s plan for a natural world. This is of course possible, but requires a huge zechus. Therefore, we need to partner with Hashem, and through our efforts, especially our efforts in tefilla, we enable the blessings to come down through non-miraculous means.

This helps explain another halacha about Bitachon – the more bitachon we have, the less effort we need to put in. This is what Rabbeinu Ovadia wrote in Etz Anaf Avot – he brought a story from the Chafetz Chaim, when people were being drafted for the army they came to him to ask what to do. The Chafetz Chaim reminded them about what it says in Avot: whoever accepts upon himself the yoke of Torah, the yoke of government will be removed from him. Rav Ovadia asks: how then so many yeshiva students are being drafted and he said that the heavenly court deals with people measure for measure – if they dedicated themselves to their Torah study with strength and unwavering commitment, without being interrupted, the yoke of government is removed completely. If they are lazy and undedicated, their acceptance of the yoke of Torah is weak and so the removal of the yoke of government is also weak.

So yes, indeed the greatest tzaddikim do indeed not have to put in any effort and can sit back and do nothing and Hashem will bless them, although this is something only one in a million can achieve. Anyone else who does this will be punished for it. The blessings that Hashem sent for them will remain for their soul in Gan Eden, but they will cause sorrow down here on earth due to not bringing the blessings down to where they were meant to go!

So, yes, we are all meant to engage in effort. We are meant to take out life insurance, go to the doctor when we are sick, teach our children a trade, and ourselves work, and not sit back and learn Torah and hope for the best. We must also make sure to put in all our effort to help our friends when they are in need and not lecture them about having bitachon. However, we must always work on our bitachon, never letting our work and efforts overshadow our Torah learning, and always remember that it is Hashem who sends the blessings and He can and will give us a good life if only we trust in Him with all our hearts. Emunah means everything is ultimately for the good, but bitachon means that we can trust that Hashem will make it good and sweet, and our prayers will come true in a way that we can visibly and tangibly see. We must remain optimistic at all times, even in the face of trouble, and certainly never panic and rush to a decision like Benei Yisrael did with the Egel!

The point of bitachon is to give us a life free of worry and anxiety, a life of tranquillity and peace. Shaar Habitachon says that anyone can have an easy life – one where we don’t have to work very much, and have a tranquil life of peace, serenity, with our families, and have our dreams come true – if only we have bitachon! The only thing stopping us from having all this is lack of bitachon. This comes from love and fear of Hashem; indeed as we saw with Benei Yisrael, bitachon is the essential ingredient for a good relationship,  most of all our relationship with Hashem – He promised to look after us, and bless us, and never abandon us – why do we doubt him?! We shouldn’t, we should be glad that He is our God and He is looking after us at all times, and love Him for it, and our bitachon will increase and we will not need anyone else, not even a malach.

We only want You Hashem! Shabbat Shalom.

I heard a very beautiful answer that also relates to a well known story in the psychology field called “the marshmallow test”. For those unfamiliar, you can read about it here https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_marshmallow_experiment As noted in that source, it was later discovered the test didn’t have so much to do with “willpower” but many other factors such as trust and security. That part is nogea to our question here.

Bnei Yisroel were in mitzrayim for a couple hundred years (210) and were steeped in a culture who worshiped nature. Everything about the Egyptian society and religion was centered around nature being divine (sun god, moon god, river god, wind god, etc). And this is why pharaoh specifically said “וַיֹּאמֶר פַּרְעֹה מִי ה” using the name Havaya (denoting above nature and time [hayah, hoveh, yihyeh]) and they were so concerned with proving the makos were a “natural” phenomenon (“this is the finger of Elokim”- elokim genatria hateva). This is the society and influence bnei Yisroel were subjected to.

So what did Hashem do? He sent signs and wonders and miracles to destroy and break this false paradigm. The issue was bnei Yisroel had trust issues due to their abuse over the generations. So Hashem had to show them. And show them again. And again. Like a parent that has to keep reaffirming their support and love and dependability to a damaged child who grew up in an unhealthy environment.

Just as a side note, we are still in golus and G-d forbid it should last another second, but I think most people (especially myself) still struggle with this. How much importance do we place on “nature” and what is “likely” to occur? How many of us can confidently walk as nachum ish gam zu and declare “gam zu letovah” for everything we encounter in this world? Being “in mitzrayim” is just as much a physical golus as a spiritual golus. And for that, Hashem is constantly and continuously creating miracles for us every second of every day and we still struggle with trust. The story of yetzias mitzrayim is just as relevant today as it was in the year 2448

questions.title_en: Why EXACTLY did Moshe make a copper snake?
questions.question:
B"H

In parshas Chukas, 5th reading, it discusses how Hashem sent snakes on the Jewish people, after they spoke out again Hashem and Moshe, because the snake, who was punished for not being able to speak at all anymore, is taking vengeance on the people who complained with their language etc, as Rashi writes:

6 G-d sent the venomous snakes against the people, and they bit the people, and many Israelites died. ו וַיְשַׁלַּ֨ח יְהֹוָ֜ה בָּעָ֗ם אֵ֚ת הַנְּחָשִׁ֣ים הַשְּׂרָפִ֔ים וַיְנַשְּׁכ֖וּ אֶת־הָעָ֑ם וַיָּ֥מָת עַם־רָ֖ב מִיִּשְׂרָאֵֽל: אֵת הַנְּחָשִׁים הַשְּׂרָפִים - The venomous snakes - i.e., that burn (שׂוֹרְפִים) a person with the poison of their teeth. אֵת הַנְּחָשִׁים הַשְּׂרָפִים. שֶׁשּׂוֹרְפִים אֶת הָאָדָם בְּאֶרֶס שִׁנֵּיהֶם: וַיְנַשְּׁכוּ אֵת הָעָם - And they bit the people. Let the snake, who was punished for slander, come and exact punishment from these people who slander; let the snake, to whom all types of food taste the same, come and exact punishment from ungrateful people for whom one thing (the manna) can have several varying tastes. וַ יְנַשְּׁכוּ אֵת הָעָם. יָבֹא נָחָשׁ שֶׁלָּקָה עַל הוֹצָאַת דִּבָּה וְיִפָּרַע מִמּוֹצִיאֵי דִּבָּה, יָבֹא נָחָשׁ שֶׁכָּל הַמִּינִין נִטְעָמִין לוֹ טַעַם אֶחָד וְיִפָּרַע מִכְּפוּיֵי טוֹבָה שֶׁדָּבָר אֶחָד מִשְׁתַּנֶּה לָהֶם לְכַמָּה מַטְעַמִּים (תנחומא):

But then, when they're being healed, Hashem told Moshe to make a snake model (without specific the material), and Moshe on his own decided to make it out of copper (נחשת), because "it's a language falling on a language" (i.e., it's a submission language to נחש, snake):

9 Moses made a copper snake and put it on a pole. If a snake had bitten a person and he looked toward the copper snake, he lived. ט וַיַּ֤עַשׂ משֶׁה֙ נְחַ֣שׁ נְח֔שֶׁת וַיְשִׂמֵ֖הוּ עַל־הַנֵּ֑ס וְהָיָ֗ה אִם־נָשַׁ֤ךְ הַנָּחָשׁ֙ אֶת־אִ֔ישׁ וְהִבִּ֛יט אֶל־נְחַ֥שׁ הַנְּח֖שֶׁת וָחָֽי: נְחַשׁ נְחשֶׁת - A copper snake. He was not told to make it from copper. However, Moses said: “The Holy One, blessed be He, calls it נָחָשׁ, and I will make it from copper (נְחֹשֶׁת), since they are similar words.” נְחַשׁ נְחשֶׁת. לֹא נֶאֱמַר לוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹתוֹ שֶׁל נְחֹשֶׁת, אֶלָּא אָמַר מֹשֶׁה, הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא קוֹרְאוֹ נָחָשׁ וַאֲנִי אֶעֱשֶׂנּוּ שֶׁל נְחֹשֶׁת, לָשׁוֹן נוֹפֵל עַל לָשׁוֹן

I was thinking about the two comments, and it seems it had something to do with fixing the mistake of the Jewish people regarding their language, that somehow through making this copper snake which has a "language falling on a language", that could rectify the negative language they spoke.

But how exactly? What is the explanation for why specifically a copper snake would fix this sin? And why did Moshe decide on his own to make it out of copper, when apparently based only on what Hashem told him, it may have been enough to just use any material for the snake?

answers.text:
Ramban on Bereshis 21:9 is not satisfied with Rashi and offers his take. The punchline is the last two paragraphs:

AND MOSES MADE ‘NECHASH NECHOSHETH’ (A SERPENT OF BRASS). “He was not told to make it of brass. But Moses said: ‘The Holy One, blessed be He, called it a nachash (serpent); therefore I will make it of nechosheth (brass) — since the one word resembles the other [in sound].” This is Rashi’s language, based upon the words of our Rabbis. (Bereshith Rabbah 31:8).

But I do not understand this, for the Holy One, blessed be He, did not mention to Moses [the word] nachash, but said to him, Make thee ‘saraf’ (a fiery serpent)! (Bamidbar 21:8). But the intention of the Sages is that Moses was guided by the substantive name thereof [which is nachash; and saraf is merely a particular description of a certain kind of serpent — a “fiery” serpent — hence he made the saraf which G-d mentioned to him from nechosheth (brass), corresponding with its substantive name].

It appears to me that the secret of this matter is that this is one of the ways of the Torah, every deed of which is a miracle within a miracle. Thus [the Torah] removes injury by means of the cause of the injury, and heals illness by means of the cause of the sickness, as the Rabbis have mentioned in connection with [the verse], and the Eternal showed him a tree (Exodus 15:25), and as occurred with the salt that Elisha [cast] into the water. (II Kings 2:21).

Now it is a well-known medical principle that all people bitten by poisonous creatures become dangerously ill when they see them, or [even] when they [only] see their likeness, so that if people who have been bitten by a mad dog or other mad animals look into water (“or any mirror.”), they see there the image of the dog or the attacker, and [this] can [cause them to] die, as is written in medical books and mentioned in the Gemara of Tractate Yoma, daf 84a. Similarly doctors protect them from [people] mentioning in their presence the name of the animal that bit them, [and they forbid people] to mention it at all, because their minds cling to this thought and do not turn away from it altogether until it causes their death.

[The doctors] have already mentioned that it is an empirical fact, amongst the wonders of reproduction, that if the urine of a person bitten by a mad dog is put in a glass receptacle after he has become rabidly sick, there will appear in that urine the likeness of the young of small dogs. And if you pass the liquid through a cloth and filter it, you will not find any trace of them at all; but if you return the liquid to the glass bottle, and it remains there for about an hour, you will again clearly see in it the small dogs. This is a true fact, and of the wonders of the powers of the soul.

Now in view of all this, it would have been correct that the Israelites, who had been bitten by the fiery serpents, should not look upon a serpent, and should not mention it or bring it to mind at all. But the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded Moses to make for them the likeness of a fiery serpent, which was [the creature] that killed them. And it is well-known that these fiery serpents have red eyes and wide heads, and their bodies at their necks are like brass. Therefore Moses could not fulfill His command to make a fiery serpent except by making a serpent of brass, which appears similar to a fiery serpent. For had he made it of any other material, it would have had the likeness of a serpent, but not that of a saraf (a fiery serpent). And the Rabbis (Bereshith Rabbah 31:8) who said [that Moses was to make a brass serpent] because “one word corresponds [in sound] to the other,” [meant to imply] that the mere mention of the name [saraf, which is a particular form of nachash, as explained above] was harmful [for the people who had been bitten, and yet G-d wanted to heal them through it].

The general intention [of this section, then] is that G-d commanded that they should be healed by the harmful agent whose nature is to kill; therefore they made its likeness in form and name, and when a person concentrated his gaze upon the brass serpent which resembled totally the offending agent, he lived. This was to make them realize that it is G-d [alone] Who sendeth death and maketh alive. (I Samuel 2:6).

A couple of answers...

First note the Sforno - The copper colour induced remorse:

נחש נחשת. אחר שהבין כונת קונו הסכים לעשותו של נחשת ולא של זהב כדי שיזכיר להם עונם מצד מראה החומר ושמו ותבניתו שעשו מעשה הנחש בהבל פיהם בדברם נגד ה' ונגד פעלו ונגד עבדו

נחש נחושת - After Moshe had understood what G-d had intended with His command, he agreed to make this replica of a snake out of copper and not out of gold. Copper would be more likely to induce thoughts of remorse as they would associate its colour with the sensation of burning.

Chizkuni - It served a functional purpose i.e.copper when shiny is highly visible

נחש נחשת לפי שהנחושת מבהיק ומבריק כענין שנאמר ונוצצים כעין נחשת קלל ואע״‎פ שמחנה ישראל היה שלש פרסאות על שלש פרסאות מי שהיה נשוך רואהו ממקומו.

נחש נחשת - “A copper snake.” This metal was chosen, as, when polished, it shines and reflects light and therefore is highly visible. We know this from Ezekiel 1,7, where the prophet describes his vision of angels whose hooflike feet were described as sparkling like burnished copper. Even though the area of the Israelites camp was three miles square, anyone who had been bitten by a snake could see the copper snake that Moses had mounted on a pole.

I posted a link to the maamar in Likkutei Torah above under a comment to the original question. I will summarize the maamar here to the best of my ability bez’H:

ויעש משה נחש נחשת To which the alter rebbe first brings the Mishnah from Rosh hashana “was it the snake that gave life or the opposite? Rather, as long as bnei Yisrael looked above and subjugated their hearts to their father in heaven…etc. על זה בזמן שישראל מסתכלין כלפי מעלה ומשעבדין את לבם לאביהם שבשמים כו׳

The alter rebbe immediately asks two questions on this Mishnah. 1) if bnei Yisrael only needed to look above, why a snake? Seemingly it would have sufficed to just put a sign on a pole that says “look up”. 2) there is a Gemara in yevamos that specifically states when a person davens he should put his eyes towards the eretz and his heart towards shamayim, seemingly contradicting our Mishnah that says they should look up and pray.

The alter rebbe begins by explaining the entire tachlis the neshama descends into a guf is to cleave to Hashem with Ahavah and yirah because this reaches the depths of a person more than machshava dibur or masseh expressed when fulfilling 613 mitzvos (which are considered levushim for the neshama). And we know, tefilah is avodah sheba lev. So therefore it follows the entire purpose of the neshama to come down into this world is for tefilah.

This answer seemingly doesn’t make sense though because before the neshama descends, it experiences infinitely greater revelation of G-dliness in the higher realms, and therefore the love and awe it feels are also infinitely higher! (Additionally during the times of the first and second Beis Hamikdash there was very little tefilah compared to what we have today-partially due to the fact tefilah is substituting for korbanos during golus). So how did they fulfill the their purpose of descending into this world ?

To this, the alter rebbe brings a Zohar that says “any person who does not transform the bitter into sweet does not have a portion in olam haba, for this is the entire purpose of creating man”. The alter rebbe explains turning bitter to sweet is “sweetening the dinim at their source”. What does that mean…?

The alter rebbe first begins by explaining everything’s source is hashem. Even things that appear bad in this world such as suffering or the like (rachmana litzlan) all have their source in hashem. It’s just when they come down through the hishtalshelus the light and goodness becomes concealed and hidden. In this way, our rabbis zl explained the term “meod” in “very good” that was said after the 6 days of creation as the malach hamaves and the yezter hara. The alter rebbe brings the mashal of the zonah hired by the king to tempt the prince. It is only to elevate the prince by revealing his inner qualities and strengths. That’s the entire purpose of a test is to elevate a person to a higher level. And the harlot who is attempting to seduce the prince is actually working for the king! Not only that, but she also wants to fail and the prince to succeed knowing how much pleasure this is going to give the king.

And this is sweetening the judgements: to understand everything that happens is hashgacha pratis and its source is good. Specifically, when a person takes this to heart the judgment itself actually changes. It’s not that the person’s perspective changed and so now the situation is good according to his new view, but the situation itself changes and becomes good.

This is most famously highlighted with the stories of nachman ish gam zu, who saw everything as good. Not that it would be good at some future time, but that it was currently good. (“Zu”=“this” denotes something physically in front of the observer that he can point to). And this in turn actually transformed the current reality (As evidenced by the fact that the dirt in the chest literally changed into the dirt of Avraham etc. see Gemara there)

So that was the message of the snake, it’s not that the snakes were bad, they were merely a conduit for building a deeper and stronger connection with Hashem. And they were sent from Hashem. And bnei Yisrael needed to look and see, this itself was actually good. And once they internalized this, the “bad” literally become the source of “life” and healing.

As for the reason they were made out of copper, the alter rebbe says from the Gemara regarding the doors of nikanor (see Yoma) “that they were the only thing in the Beis Hamikdash that was not replaced with gold. And some say they shone even more brilliantly than gold.” Copper changes color when hit by the sun. So too do our challenges and struggles change from sorrows rachmana litzlan to newfound levels of divine connection and blessings when we connect with The Source.

questions.title_en: Does a store need to honor gift cards sold by a previous store which went bankrupt?
questions.question:
If you bought a gift card from store A, which then goes bankrupt, with store B then selling the original material, does store B have to honor the original gift card sold by store A?

(I was told that Reb Moshe says yes. Where is that teshuvah located?)

answers.text:
It is impossible to give a definite answer without knowing the details. This is likely to be highly dependent on

  1. the terms of the purchase agreement between store B and store A. In some cases, the terms cover only the purchase of the stock and rental agreement, in others, it might be a full takeover of the business with all its debts. In the first case, the gift card wouldn't be covered, in the second, it would
  2. the law of the land, in case it prescribes a certain set of mandatory behaviors (e.g., to honor the previous store's debts if you continue their business)

This being said, R Moshe Feinstein addresses business bankruptcies in Igrot Moshe CM II:62 where he emphasizes the need to apply the law of the land. Specifically there he forbids the owner from repaying certain debts ahead of others and favoring certain debt-holders.

questions.title_en: Samson is Marked for Punishment for Following his Eyes Before He is Described as Actually Following his Eyes - Why?
questions.question:
Judges 14:

וַיֹּ֨אמֶר ל֜וֹ אָבִ֣יו וְאִמּ֗וֹ הַאֵין֩ בִּבְנ֨וֹת אַחֶ֤יךָ וּבְכׇל־עַמִּי֙ אִשָּׁ֔ה כִּֽי־אַתָּ֤ה הוֹלֵךְ֙ לָקַ֣חַת אִשָּׁ֔ה מִפְּלִשְׁתִּ֖ים הָעֲרֵלִ֑ים וַיֹּ֨אמֶר שִׁמְשׁ֤וֹן אֶל־אָבִיו֙ אוֹתָ֣הּ קַֽח־לִ֔י כִּי־הִ֖יא יָשְׁרָ֥ה בְעֵינָֽי׃
His father and mother said to him, “Is there no one among the daughters of your own kindred and among all our people, that you must go and take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?” But Samson answered his father, “Get me that one, for she is the one that pleases me.”

Then he meets her and is described as:

וַיֵּ֖רֶד וַיְדַבֵּ֣ר לָֽאִשָּׁ֑ה וַתִּישַׁ֖ר בְּעֵינֵ֥י שִׁמְשֽׁוֹן׃
Then he went down and spoke to the woman, and she pleased Samson.

This means that he is described later on as finding her pleasing - after he said that she was pleasing.

The Talmud imputes guilt to Samson as the get-go (Sota 9b):

גְּמָ׳ תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: שִׁמְשׁוֹן בְּעֵינָיו מָרַד, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״וַיֹּאמֶר שִׁמְשׁוֹן אֶל אָבִיו אוֹתָהּ קַח לִי כִּי הִיא יָשְׁרָה בְעֵינָי״ — לְפִיכָךְ נִקְּרוּ פְּלִשְׁתִּים אֶת עֵינָיו, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״וַיֹּאחֲזוּהוּ פְלִשְׁתִּים וַיְנַקְּרוּ אֶת עֵינָיו״.
GEMARA: The Sages taught (Tosefta 3:15): Samson rebelled with his eyes, as it is stated: “Then his father and his mother said to him: Is there never a woman among the daughters of your brethren, or among all my people, that you go out to take a wife of the uncircumcised Philistines? And Samson said to his father: Get her for me; for she is pleasant in my eyes” (Judges 14:3). Therefore, the Philistines gouged out his eyes, as it is stated: “And the Philistines laid hold on him, and put out his eyes” (Judges 16:21).

Thus, Samson is already guilty of following his eyes at the moment he said she was pleasing even though the story has not yet described him as coming to that realization himself.

The Talmud thus finds him guilty of following his eyes from the get-go (the first mention in the Psukim).

אִינִי? וְהָכְתִיב: ״וְאָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ לֹא יָדְעוּ כִּי מֵה׳ הִיא״. כִּי אֲזַל מִיהָא — בָּתַר יַשְׁרוּתֵיהּ אֲזַל.
The Gemara asks: Is that so? But isn’t it written: “But his father and his mother knew not that it was from the Lord; as he sought a subterfuge against the Philistines” (Judges 14:4), indicating that Samson’s searching for a Philistine wife was due to a Divine mission? The Gemara answers: Although God did plan the punishment of the Philistines, in any event when he went, he followed his inclination and did not act for the sake of Heaven.

Why is he characterized as following his eyes before being described as finding her pleasing in his eyes?

questions.title_he: What is the commentary שדה צופים on the Rosh?
questions.question:
Curiosity got the better of me and I was looking in the back of the Gemara Megilah at the Rosh to see what he says. Then I noticed that there is a commentary on the Rosh called שדה צופים. All it does is quote the Rosh in other places in shas.

My question is why? When was it written? And why is it called that name?

Any other trivia is welcome as well.

answers.text:
A little bit of digging led to me find on the Otzar Website here that the author was the Dayan and Rosh Yeshiva Rabbi Bezalel Ronsburg/Ranschburg who lived 1760-1820.

According to here:

He devoted himself to commenting on those tractates of the Talmud on which there are few commentaries, such as his Horah Gever on *Horayot (Prague, 1802) and Pitḥei Niddah (1957; published in Jerusalem 1928 under the title Hokhmat Beẓalel). His Sedeh Zofim on *Asher b. Jehiel's halakhot was appended to the Prague Talmud edition (1839–46). His Ma'aseh Rav (Prague, 1823) deals partly with tractate Nazir. *Haggahot based on it are included in all subsequent editions of the Talmud. Many letters on halakhic subjects which he wrote to the censor Carolus Fischer (partly signed "Ilan Shoshan") are preserved in the Prague University Library (mgwj, 62 (1918), 49–56).

  • "Asher b. Jehiel" (Asher ben Yechiel) is the Rosh.

questions.title_en: Must a gadol have two pubic hairs?
questions.question:
According to Mishna Niddah, for a male to have the halachic status of a גדול (an adult obligated in the mitzvot), he must be over 13 years old, and have at least two pubic hairs.

Anecdotally, I have never seen a case where the second condition had practical ramifications (e.g. a late-developing boy having his בר מצְוה ceremony postponed, or not being counted in a Minyan, etc). Personally, when I turned 13, nobody asked me whether I had pubic hair before allowing me to say a ברכה on the Torah, or to say קִדּוּשׁ, or to count in an Minyan, and so on.

Does the second condition still apply today? Does a child need to have pubic hair before being considered a גדול?

answers.text:
See Pitchei Teshuva on Shulchan Aruch Yoreh Deah 1:11

שנעשה בר מצוה. עי' במג"א סל"ט סק"א דבדבר דקטן פסול מדאורייתא בעינן שיהא גדול ממש דהיינו שהביא ב' שערות אחר שהוא בן י"ג שנה ועי' ברמ"א שם סימן נ"ה ס"ה דלמידי דרבנן סומכין על החזקה שהביא ב"ש ע"ש. ומזה נלמוד לנדון זה דאף אחר יג"ש ויום א' אסור לשחוט לצורך אכילה מאחר שהוא פסול מדאורייתא או מטעמא דהלבוש שאינו בר זביחה או מטעמא דהש"ך שאינו בר עדות אם אין אחר עומד על גביו עד שיוודע שהביא ב"ש או שהוא בן ל"ה שנה ויום א' (ומ"ש המג"א עד שיהא בן י"ח שנה כבר תמהו עליו האחרונים) או שנתמלא זקנו כמבואר בח"מ סל"ה

I'll translate the parts in bold:

See Magen Avraham [Orach Chaim] 39:1, where something that a minor would be Biblically disqualified, it is required that he be an actual adult, i.e. have 2 pubic hairs after they are 13 years old. And see the Rema in 55:5 where if it is a Rabbinical matter, we can rely on the assumption that he has 2 pubic hairs...[Alternatively, he is considered an adult even without pubic hair] once he reaches 35 years and one day, or has a full beard, as is explained in Choshen Mishpat 35[:1]

questions.title_en: How does an unmarried woman nurse children?
questions.question:
In Avodah Zarah 26a, the gemara provides two excuses that a woman might give if asked by a non-Jewish woman to nurse her baby. She can say that she desires to get married, so does not want anybody to see her nursing, and she can also say (if she already is married) that she does not wish to become repulsive to her husband.

I am wondering how an unmarried woman nurses a child. Is the implication that she had a baby but its father died or divorced her? Or is the passage predicated on a belief that women could nurse children without having first given birth themselves?

answers.text:
The gemara does not say anything about her being embarrassed to be seen nursing. I also don't see that implied in the commentaries. All I see is a very "diplomatic" statement that covers all possibilities.

I want to get married.

This carries everything:

  1. I have never had a baby so I cannot lactate.
  2. Even if I could lactate, I don't want to harm my prospects of getting married.

Possibility 2 covers all cases:

  • She already has a baby and that would embarrass her
  • It would not embarrass her to reveal she had a baby, but it would otherwise disrupt her prospects of getting married
  • They did know how to induce lactation back then

So, the excuse the gemara provides for single women is designed to be diplomatic and cover all possibilities without implying any of them, and without causing enmity.

I don't understand the question. Yes, the Talmud was dealing with reality, and not suggesting something that does not accord with reality. The passage in question:

סָבַר רַב יוֹסֵף לְמֵימַר: אוֹנוֹקֵי בְּשָׂכָר שְׁרֵי מִשּׁוּם אֵיבָה. אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: יָכְלָה לְמֵימַר, אִי פְּנוּיָה הִיא — ״בָּעֵינָא לְאִינְּסוֹבֵי״, אִי אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ הִיא — ״לָא קָא מִזְדַּהַמְנָא בְּאַפֵּי גַּבְרַאי״.

Rav Yosef also thought to say: Nursing the child of a gentile woman in exchange for payment is permitted due to enmity. Abaye said to him: The concern of enmity does not apply, because she can say, if she is unmarried: I wish to get married. And if she is a married woman, she may say: I do not wish to become repulsive to my husband. Since she can provide a reasonable excuse for refusing to nurse a gentile child, the concern of enmity does not apply.

That is, a woman who can nurse, and perhaps has functioned as a wetnurse in the past, is approached to be employed by a gentile woman. This is targeting women who can nurse, not all women in the world. Abaye explains how there would be no enmity caused by refusal, because of a credible excuse. For those women who are not married, they would say X; for those who are married, they would say Y.

So yes, we would read the gemara in a way that conforms to reality, that there are some unmarried women who are wetnurses. That could arise due to out-of-wedlock pregnancies, or a woman who was divorced or widowed. Indeed, this newfound singlehood might have not even occurred recently, as a wetnurse who continues in the profession without pause can do so for years. Abaye said this to comprehensively cover all cases, so that there is no enmity in a subset of cases.
