questions.title_he: What Does the Ramad Vali Mean by "the Form/Shape of the crucified ... כל מיני טומאה ...גיהנם שולטים בו"?
questions.question:
The Ramad Vali states that the form/shape of the crucified is that which כל מיני טומאה ... גיהנם שולטים בו. How?

https://hebrewbooks.org/pdfpager.aspx?req=51267&st=&pgnum=255&hilite=

answers.text:
I searched and found this answer:

https://hebrewbooks.org/pdfpager.aspx?req=51270&st=&pgnum=127&hilite=

In sum, the Torah in Devarim states “And if a man has committed a crime punishable by death and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree, his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall bury him the same day, for a hanged man is cursed by God.'

Thus the image of a dead man suspended on wood is a cursed thing too (a metaphor for a tree of death).

questions.title_en: Why was there a clear impact on Klal Yisrael after the deaths of Miriam and Aharon, but not Moshe Rabbeinu's?
questions.question:
Juxtaposed with Miriam's death (Bamidbar 20:1 ff) is the be’er stopping and the people complaining.

Following Aharon's death (Bamidbar 20:29 ff) Klal Yisrael becomes exposed to enemy attack.

Chazal see a causal nexus between these events.

However, when Moshe Rabbeinu is niftar (Devarim 34:5 ff), there's no detectable fallout.

Given that Moshe was the greatest of the three, why isn’t there any noticeable effect right after his petirah?

(Clarification: I'm aware of this gemara. I'm looking for something more peshat oriented; I'm only going with Chazal insofar as Aharon and Miriam's deaths have a devastating effect, which seems to be the case according to peshat as well)

questions.title_en: Using tablets of law as a car decoration
questions.question: Would it be acceptable to use decorative tablets of law as a hood ornament or other decoration as described in Chaim Potok's Book of Lights?

answers.text:
As no one has answered so far, I'll post my comment as an answer:

I wouldn't use anything with the full text of the Ten Commandments. If it just says 'Alef Bet Gimel' -- something like the US military's symbol for it chaplains:

Personally I'd find it a little tacky, unless someone needed people to know they carried out a religious role. (Parking in the "reserved for clergy" spot at the hospital, for instance.) Otherwise, why are you shouting it out to the world? Tacky ... but I can't say "unacceptable."

The Talmud talks quite a bit about yuhara, the notion that it's wrong for an average person to walk around trying to look like they're a pious sage. There's even a funny story of a fellow who got arrested for wearing a style of clothing only associated with pious sages ... who was able to prove he was, in fact, enough of a sage, and therefore was released.

That's about a hood ornament, which is basically you shouting it to others.

If you want to put it inside the car as a decoration ... again a generic "tablets" symbol like this, without the full text ... if you like it, fine; again, not something I really see a lot of Jews do. But there's no sanctity to a symbol like that, so if it makes you happy, why not. (I definitely have seen car interiors adorned with the text of the Wayfarer's Prayer, but that's a little different.)

questions.title_he: Does להתעטף cover טליתות קטנות if none are worn
questions.question:
Some have the minhag to refrain from making a bracha upon donning a טלית קטן when getting dressed in the morning, but to have it—and all טליתות קטנות that one might wear throughout the day—in mind during the Bracha over the טלית גדול.

If one doesn’t don a טלית קטן in the morning, would the Bracha over the טלית גדול still cover any טליתות קטנות he might wear throughout the day?

answers.text:
The Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 9:10

הַפּוֹשֵׁט טַלִּיתוֹ וְדַעְתּוֹ לַחֲזֹר וּלְלָבְשׁוֹ מִיָּד, אֲפִלּוּ הָלַךְ לְבֵית הַכִּסֵּא, כְּשֶׁחוֹזֵר וְלוֹבְשׁוֹ, לֹא יְבָרֵךְ עָלָיו If you take off your tallis with the intention of putting it on again immediately, even if you did so for the purpose of going to the lavatory, when you return and put it on again you do not recite the berachah over it (the tallis).

If you can't take it off and go do other things without needing another bracha, you definitely can't exempt a different tallit that wasn't ever worn.

questions.title_en: Biblical events marked by day of week
questions.question:
Many events in the Tanakh are dated by day/month/year, but I don't recall events explicitly said to fall on a certain day of the week (except for the Mekoshesh).

Are there any?

NB, The days of creation don't count.

answers.text: The text of the TaNaKh does not mention any day of the week except for Friday and Shabbos as I checked doing search. No specific event is recorded with its day of the week. There are generic events which occured or could have occured for a period of several weeks, such as people getting a double portion of manna Shemos 16:22 on Friday, or violations of Shabbos Nechemiah 13:15-17 among others.

questions.title_en: How can a Sotah profit from sinning?
questions.question:
A Sotah is a woman who went into seclusion with someone after her husband warned her not to go into seclusion with that man. This is a sin.

If a Sotah didn’t do a sexual act while in seclusion, she is rewarded with having children.

We know there a concept in Gemara that a sinner can’t profit. So how can this lady be rewarded with children as a consequence of sinning by going into seclusion?

answers.text:
The Divrei Cheifetz (end of top paragraph) answering a different but related question, suggests that having children is not a reward per se, but rather a natural consequence of the humiliation the accused woman undergoes during the sotah process. He cites the principle of Chazal that inability to have children is one of the things which depends on mazal, not on merit. When someone undergoes great embarrassment Chazal say that on some level they experience death. If so, he writes, their mazal is automatically reset and the old mazal that was stopping them from having children is removed.

(If something is a natural consequence rather than a reward, it does not fall into the category of not rewarding the sinner. To illustrate: if someone robs a bank, they may profit from their sin, but it doesn't contradict this principle because they are not being rewarded, the fact that they have the stolen money is just a natural result).

However, as @Nahum pointed out, this answer will not suffice for the opinion in the Gemara that women who can already have children but with a painful childbirth will now be able to have easier births, etc.

The Divrei Mussar offers a different approach. He writes that there is a principle in Chazal that Hashem does not hold back reward even for someone steeped in sin. This woman who defied her husband to be together with this man, and yet held herself back from sinning, is deserving of some reward for her great restraint, even in the context of her previous failures. When she undergoes the humiliation of the Sotah process, this atones for the sin of secluding with the man. But the zchus of holding back and not completing her sin is still there to be rewarded.

Perhaps it can be explained based off of another comment by Chazal brought in Rashi to Bamidbar 5:12 that if one withholds what should be given to the kohen then he will end up going to the kohen with his sotah wife in tow (as the kohen is the one that administers the process).

Now, why would someone withhold matnos kehunah? He may not recognize what the kohen is doing for him or doesn't appreciate it enough that he feels the need to support him for it. Or he may be downright miserly and tight-fisted. Whatever the exact reason, these middos, brought over to the home front with regard to his wife, will no doubt have a devastating effect on their relationship. His wife will not feel appreciated, treasured, loved, worthy of her husband spending his money on her and on and on. She will then potentially be open to a more generous and attentive man's attentions.

It turns out that to some extent the husband is to blame, for through his mistreatment of his wife he is pushing her to do things she would otherwise not consider doing.

Therefore, if she doesn't actually commit adultery it makes sense that she receives some compensation for being put through the wringer of the sotah ordeal, as she was somewhat responding to her husband's mistreatment.

(See here for more.)

While it is of course true that she shouldn't have secluded herself especially with a man that her husband specifically cautioned her regarding, however, once she did, with the ostensible purpose of committing adultery, it is also true that during the seclusion she resisted the enormous pull and desire she has for the man, overcoming the strong attraction she feels toward him.

Although it was certainly wrong of her to seclude herself with him initially and while it was definitely a mess of her own making still and all she did ultimately avoid acting carnally on her feelings and it is for not taking it to the next level that she is rewarded.

Compare it to say someone that goes to a brothel but at the last minute leaves before committing the sin.

questions.title_en: Why is Shimon ben Gamliel missing his honorific?
questions.question:
In mAvot 1:17 Shimon the son of Raban Gamliel (see previous mishna) is not given the title Raban like his father or grandson (see subsequent mishna). I would like to understand why this is.

When I learned this mishna as a child I was told that R' Shimon ben Gamliel (RSbG) was martyred when he was young and had not attained the age of ordination. However, it seems RSbG did in fact serve as the Nasi as per a braita in bShabbat 15a

וְהָתַנְיָא: הִלֵּל וְשִׁמְעוֹן, גַּמְלִיאֵל וְשִׁמְעוֹן, נָהֲגוּ נְשִׂיאוּתָן לִפְנֵי הַבַּיִת מֵאָה שָׁנָה.
Hillel, and his son Shimon, and his grandson Gamliel, and his great-grandson Shimon filled their position of Nasi before the House, while the Temple was standing, for a hundred years

I am aware that the commentary of Tiferet Yisrael (R' Lifshitz, among others) posits that RSbG made this statement before he was appointed at Nasi and hence the absence (similar to Machzor Vitri). I am not sure how this information could be known and would like to explore other answers.

questions.title_en: Help finding source - Avraham, Ur Kasdim, and the Fire of Gehenom
questions.question:
Below is a tweet from Josh Rosenfeld (@shuaros) on October 19, 2016:

Avraham forced out of Ur Kasdim against his will/wanted to prepare for pain of Gehinnom/so he could remain there to save his children
~תפא״ש

What is the original source for this idea? Or at least, what sefer is referenced by the rashei teivot at the bottom?

answers.text:
Thank you user "Sholom" for the answer - Tiferet Shlomo, Sukkot, section 17.

ואברהם עודנו עומד לפני ד'. דהנה ידוע גודל מעלת אברהם אבינו ע"ה במסירות נפש לד' ותוקף אהבתו ותשוקתו לעשות רצונו להאבד הוא וכל מאודו לכבוד השם יתעלה. וכל הימים הי' משתוקק ומצפה מתי יגיע לידו איזה נסיון להמסר נפשו להאבד על קדושת שמו ע"כ בפ' העקידה כתיב וישכם אברהם בבקר. כוונתו להשכים בבקר למהר ולבצע את מעשהו לשחוט את בנו יחידו מיד כי ירא פן אח"כ לא יגיע לידו ולא יקום מחשבתו לקיים המצוה הזאת לבצע מעשהו וכאשר הי' באמת הדיבור אל תשלח ידך אל הנער. וכן באור כשדים כתיב והוצאתו מאור כשדים ר"ל בע"כ כי לא רצה לצאת מהכבשן בראותו כי לא נשרף והי' מתעכב והולך בו פן ישרף ומצפה על זה לכבוד הש"י עד שהוציאו הקב"ה בעצמו בע"כ וזהו אשר הוצאתיך מאור כשדים. והנה מסירות נפש ותוקף האהבה לד' היא העומדת לבניו אחריו בכל דור ודור לבטל מהם כל גזירות קשות כמ"ש ויעקד את יצחק בנו הוא הטובה שהיתה לישראל כי עקד כל נשמות ישראל עמו. וזה וישם את בנו ממעל לעצים ר"ל למעלה מבחי' עץ הדעת ועי"ז נתקנו. וז"ש ואברהם עודנו עומד כמ"ש חכז"ל כי אברהם אבינו ע"ה עומד על פתחו של גיהנם וכו':

And Abraham still stands before God. Thus is known the greatness of the virtue of our forefather Abraham, ע"ה, in his devotion to God, and the strength of his love and desire to do His will, even to perish, and with all his resources, for the glory of God, may He be exalted. And all the days he longed and awaited for whichever test to surrender His soul to perish for the sanctity of His Name. Therefore, in the Story on Akkeidah it is written, "And Abraham awoke in the morning." His intention was to get up early in the morning to hurry and carry out his deed of slaughtering his only son immediately, because he feared that later he would not be able to do so and that his mind would not arise to fulfill this commandment to carry out his deed, and when it's later written, "do not lay your hand on the boy." And so it is written in the Ur of Chaldeans, that God took him out of the Ur of the Chaldeans. The intent to say, because he did not want to come out of the furnace when he saw that he was not burned, and he delayed and walked in it, lest he burn up in honor of the God until the Holy One, blessed be He, brought him out Himself from Ur of Chaldeans. And that is why it's written "He brought him out of the Ur of Chaldeans". And his (Abraham's) dedication of the soul and the strength of the love for God stands for his sons after him in every generation to abolish from them all harsh decrees, as it says, "And he bound Isaac his son," that is the good that was to Israel, because he bound all the souls of Israel with him. And this, and "he placed his son upon the pieces of wood", means to say, above the test of the tree of knowledge, and this way it was established. "And Abraham still stood" that why חז"ל say Bereshis Rabba 48:8, "For Abraham our father, may God bless him, stands at the entrance of Gehenna, etc."

questions.title_en: Non-Jewish attestation of Torah Judaism's moral superiority
questions.question:
Since the Babylonian exile, through Greek and Roman civilizations, Christendom, and the Islamic world, what are some non-Jewish sources that recognize the superiority of Jewish morality?

For example, transcendental monotheism, observing the Sabbath, dietary laws, interpersonal laws, charity and philanthropy, criminal law, and others.

answers.text:
John Adams, the second United States President, is quoted as saying:

I will insist that the Hebrews have done more to civilize Men than any other Nation. If I were an Atheist and believed in blind eternal Fate, I should Still believe that Fate had ordained the Jews to be the most essential Instrument for civilizing the Nations. If I were an Atheist of the other Sect, who believe or pretend to believe that all is ordered by Chance, I Should believe that Chance had ordered the Jews to preserve and propagate, to all Mankind the Doctrine of a Supreme intelligent wise, almighty Sovereign of the Universe, which I believe to be the great essential Principle of all Morality and consequently of all Civilization.

questions.title_en: What are the differences between the assorted GR"A related siddurim
questions.question:
The following siddurim purport to be attempts at constructing a siddur around the GR"A's nusach and teachings, though information on them is scarce and often conflicting.

  • Ishei Yisrael -- אשי ישראל

  • Siddur Vilna -- סידור וולנא

  • Siddur HaGra - B'Nigleh Ve'Nistar -- סידור הגר׳׳א בנגלה ובנסתר

  • Ezor Eliyahu -- אזור אליהו

  • Aliyot Eliyahu -- עליות אליהו

Other answers on this site have discussed that Ezor Eliyahu is a popular siddur among the followers of the GR"A, and that it was revised into Aliyot Eliyahu, though I may have misunderstood that comment, which is why I have labeled them separately. I believe Ishei Yisrael is a yet older version, which may have been revised into Ezor Eliyahu.

I have never heard anyone mention Siddur Vilna, nor Siddur HaGRA B'Nigleh Ve'Nistar.

I believe the B'Nigleh Ve'Nistar version is a siddur with footnotes on the GR"A mysticism, so its reason for separation and printing are clear.

Do any of these siddurim contain differences in the davened prayers, or are the differences are entirely paratextual? If so, what does their paratext focus on, eg: what's the motivation for the siddur's distinction? A blog post: "The Perils of Ignoring Precedent: Alterations in the Kaddish Prayer" seems to hint that the three sidurrim I have lumped together (Ishei Yisrael -> Ezor Eliyahu -> Aliyot Eliyahu) do contain slight liturgical differences, though I'm not certain.

Does anyone have concrete information or sources to share on the liturgical and or paratextual differences between these related siddurim?

questions.title_he: Does אפי תלתא apply to someone who is dead?
questions.question:
The Chofetz Chaim Hilchos Lashon Hara 2:2 states:

וּמַה שֶּׁנִּמְצָּא הֶתֵּר בְּדִבְרֵי חֲזַ"ל לוֹמַר בִּפְנִי שְׁלֹשָה, הַיְנוּ בְּדָבָר שֶׁאֵינֶנּוּ גְּנַאי גָּמוּר וְהַדִּבּוּר שֶׁלּוֹ יֵשׁ לוֹ שְׁנִי פָּנִים. וְעִנְיָן כָּזֶה יָדוּעַ שֶׁתָּלוּי לְפִי הַדִּבּוּר, שֶׁאוֹמֵר אוֹתוֹ הַמְסַפֵּר בְּעֵת סִפּוּרוֹ, בָּזֶה הִתִּירוּהוּ חֲזַ"ל לוֹמַר בִּפְנֵי שְׁלֹשָה וְתָלוּהוּ, כֵּיוָן שֶׁאוֹמֵר הַדְּבָרִים בִּפְנִי שְׁלֹשָה, יוֹדֵעַ בְּוַדַּאי שֶׁיָּבוֹאוּ הַדְּבָרִים לְאָזְנָיו, דְּחַבְרָךְ חבְרָא אִית לֵה {שחברך חבר יש לו}, וְעַל כֵּן הוּא שׁוֹמֵר אֶת עַצְּמוֹ בְּעֵת אֲמִירָה לוֹמַר, בְּאֹפֶן שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה מִנְכָּר מִלְּשׁוֹנוֹ לְשׁוֹן גְּנַאי.

As to there being found a heter [a halachic permit] in the words of Chazal to speak it before three, this applies to something which is not an absolute taint and which can be understood in two ways. It is well known that such things depend on how they are said. It is such a thing that Chazal permitted to say in the presence of three, the rationale being that since he says it before three, he knows for a certainty that these things will come to his [the object's] ears (for "your friend has a friend, etc."). The speaker, therefore, heeds himself in speaking, that what he says will not be understood negatively.

If the principle is that it could potentially get back to the person about whom it was said, does this principle hold when that person is dead? There is no way it will get back to that person.

questions.title_en: Is it Chukat Hagoy to stand for a Kallah?
questions.question: Is it chukat hagoy to stand for a bride when she walks down the aisle?

answers.text:
There is some disagreement regarding Chukat Hagoyim regarding instances when we have a specific practical reason to do something that also happens to be done by the goyim. For example, the Rema (O"C 494) cites a custom to adorn the Shul with greenery on Shavuot. The Gra held that it is forbidden to do so because the Goyim similarly decorate their houses of worship (there is discussion about what kinds of greenery were forbidden by the Gra). Some poskim disagree with the Gra on the grounds that if we have our own reason to do something, then it cannot be considered Chukat Hagoyim (see for example Daat Torah O"C 494). In the case of standing for the Kallah, there has been a reason given, which according to this opinion would then take it out of the category of Chukat Hagoyim:

The Mishnah relates that when people would come to bring the bikkurim, the people in Jerusalem would stop what they were doing and stand up. Rav Ovadiah Mebartenura explains they did this out of respect for those engaged in a mitzvah. He writes that this principle applies to certain other mitzvot as well, such as carrying a coffin to burial and carrying a baby to the bris milah. There are those who suggest that this is the basis for the practice to stand when the Chattan and Kallah walk down the aisle.

questions.title_en: Talmud Bavli - Moses is Heman?
questions.question:
In the Babylonian Talmud Bava Basra 15a, it is reported that Rav said Heman, mentioned in 1 Kings 5:11, is the same person as Moses.

קָא חָשֵׁיב מֹשֶׁה וְקָא חָשֵׁיב הֵימָן, וְהָאָמַר רַב: הֵימָן זֶה מֹשֶׁה – כְּתִיב הָכָא: ״הֵימָן״, וּכְתִיב הָתָם: ״בְּכׇל בֵּיתִי נֶאֱמָן הוּא״! תְּרֵי הֵימָן הֲווֹ.

The Gemara asks: The baraita counts Moses among the ten elders whose works are included in the book of Psalms, and it also counts Heman. But doesn’t Rav say: The Heman mentioned in the Bible (I Kings 5:11) is the same person as Moses? This is proven by the fact that it is written here: “Heman” (Psalms 88:1), which is Aramaic for trusted, and it is written there about Moses: “For he is the trusted one in all My house” (Numbers 12:7). The Gemara answers: There were two Hemans, one of whom was Moses, and the other a Temple singer from among the descendants of Samuel.

How is this possible?

answers.text:
First off, the original text of the Talmud does not specify 1 Kings 5:11. That is the interpolated English commentary from Rav Adin Steinsaltz, and based on Rashi ad loc. It might be absolutely correct as an interpretation, but clarity is important. All the Talmud literally says is (translated):

But doesn’t Rav say: Heman is Moses.

To expand on Rav's approach to certain Biblical books, I would point to Vayikra Rabba 1:3:

רַבִּי סִימוֹן בְּשֵׁם רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי וְרַבִּי חָמָא אֲבוּהָ דְּרַבִּי הוֹשַׁעְיָא בְּשֵׁם רַב, אָמְרֵי, לֹא נִתַּן דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים אֶלָּא לִדָּרֵשׁ...

Rabbi Simon, in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and Rabbi Ḥama father of Rabbi Hoshaya, in the name of Rav, said: Chronicles was given only for expounding...

He goes on to show certain absolute contradictions between Divrei Hayamim (Chronicles) and other narratives. The idea seems to be that we should not look to the plain meaning of such verses. Rather, the only purpose of such verses is as coded references, conveying some deep midrashic meaning. As I have argued elsewhere in the past, this idea of לא ניתן אלא / "it was only given for" could be understood as that it was only canonized in respect to its midrashic meaning. Therefore, we should not be troubled with contradictions with other Biblical books.

That midrash in Vayikra Rabba, from Rav, goes on to interpret this verse (I Chronicles 4:18):

“His Judahite wife bore Yered father of Gedor, [Ḥever father of Sokho, and Yekutiel father of Zano'aḥ; these are the sons of Bitya daughter of Pharaoh whom Mered took as a wife]”

such that many of the names in the verse are actually coded references to Moshe and aspects of his personality.

Heiman is presumably another instance of Rav interpreting a verse in this way.

Now, which Heiman verse is being referenced regarding the identification of הֵימָן זֶה מֹשֶׁה? Rav Steinsaltz, following Rashi, says that it is I Melachim 5:11 that refers to Moshe:

He was wiser than anybody else—including Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, Chalkol, and Darda the sons of Mahol. His fame spread among all the surrounding nations.

But other verses also refer to this same Heiman, such as I Divrei Hayamim 2:6:

וּבְנֵ֣י זֶ֗רַח זִ֠מְרִ֠י וְאֵיתָ֧ן וְהֵימָ֛ן וְכַלְכֹּ֥ל וָדָ֖רַע כֻּלָּ֥ם חֲמִשָּֽׁה׃ {ס}

The sons of Zerah: Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Dara, five in all.

As Rashi on that verse in Melachim notes, there is a Midrash Aggadah that goes through the people in the verse. Even so, I don't think that is predicated on the verse in Melachim but on a different verse in Divrei Hayamim. Again, we can look to Vayikra Rabba 9:1, where I can excerpt:

דִכְתִיב (דברי הימים א ב, ו): וּבְנֵי זֶרַח זִמְרִי וְאֵיתָן וְהֵימָן וְכַלְכֹּל [ודרע] [ודרדע] כֻּלָּם חֲמִשָּׁה, זִמְרִי, רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי אָמַר זֶה עָכָן, וְלָמָּה קוֹרְאוֹ זִמְרִי, שֶׁעָשָׂה כְּמַעֲשֵׂה זִמְרִי. וְרַבָּנָן אָמְרֵי שֶׁנִּזַּמְּרוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל עַל יָדוֹ. אֵיתָן זֶה אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עַל שֵׁם (תהלים פט, א): מַשְׂכִּיל לְאֵיתָן הָאֶזְרָחִי. הֵימָן זֶה משֶׁה, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (במדבר יב, ז): בְּכָל בֵּיתִי נֶאֱמָן הוּא. רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָן אָמַר זֶה עָכָן, עַל שֵׁם (יהושע ז, כ): אָמְנָה אָנֹכִי חָטָאתִי. כַּלְכֹּל זֶה יוֹסֵף, עַל שֵׁם (בראשית מז, יב): וַיְכַלְכֵּל יוֹסֵף. [ודרע] [ודרדע] זֶה דּוֹר הַמִּדְבָּר שֶׁכֻּלּוֹ דֵּעָה. כֻּלָּם חֲמִשָּׁה, וְכִי אֵין אָנוּ יוֹדְעִים שֶׁכֻּלָּם חֲמִשָּׁה, אֶלָּא מְלַמֵּד שֶׁאַף עָכָן הָיָה עִמָּהֶן לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא,

That is what is written: “The sons of Zeraḥ: Zimri, Eitan, Heiman, Kalkol, and Darda; all of them were five” (I Chronicles 2:6). Zimri – Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: This is Akhan, as he performed the act of Zimri. The Rabbis say: It is because Israel was pruned [nizmeru] on his account. Eitan – this is Abraham our patriarch, based on: “A contemplation by Eitan the Ezrahite” (Psalms 89:1). Heiman – this is Moses, as it is stated: “In all My household he is trusted [ne’eman]” (Numbers 12:7). Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥman said: This is Akhan, based on: “Indeed [omna], I have sinned” (Joshua 7:20). Kalkol – this is Joseph, based on: “Joseph sustained [vaykhalkel]” (Genesis 47:12). Darda – this is the generation [dor] of the wilderness, which was full of knowledge [de’a]. “All of them were five” – do we not know that all of them were five? Rather, it teaches that even Akhan was with them in the World to Come.

The verse that mentions כֻּלָּם חֲמִשָּׁה is the one in Divrei Hayamim. Thus, this seems to be the similar approach of interpreting that names that appear in Divrei Hayamim, rather than taking them in the straightforward peshat meaning.

Not sure what's bothering you. Two different people named Heiman.

The point in Bava Basra is to really expand on King Solomon's wisdom.

"He was even wiser than Ethan the Ezrachite, Heiman, Kalkol, and Darda, people of Machol."

If these are just random people from his time who were smart, eh okay. The Midrashic reading, however, is that all of these names are coded references to great leaders before King Solomon, which would therefore make King Solomon sound a whole lot greater:

"He was even wiser than [Abraham], who was mighty [in spreading monotheism] and yet a good citizen [as he showed respect to those around him]; and [Moses], the faithful one [as "meheimna" is Aramaic for "faithful"]; and [Joseph], the sustainer/provider [for the ancient Middle East during the famine], and the whole generation who knew G-d's presence intensely while witnessing miracles in the desert, the people who achieved forgiveness.

So yes, there was a literal Heiman, a Levite Temple chorister; but the verse in Kings is giving a coded reference to Moses. Whether the verse intended both literally the chorister and, if you read between the lines, Moses; or was only intending for Moses ... is a question of whether that homiletic line in the Talmud is intended as the interpretation, or another level of interpretation. (Both approaches are acceptable.)

questions.title_en: What does the word ‘Ashtaroth’ mean in the Talmudic context?
questions.question: There are several interpretations of the word. I would like to know the meaning of the word ‘Ashtaroth’ in the Talmudic context. example of Talmudic source: Chulin 84 b.

answers.text:
in this case in chillin the gamora is making a play on words. It says ashteros like flocks of sheep, and then it says it as enrichment (from ashir) to make a colloquialism that flocks enrich their shepherd. Ramban has many rayos of the history of this word on devarim 1:4.

hope this helps:

אֲשֶׁר יוֹשֵׁב בְּחֶשְׁבּוֹן, שֶׁלֹּא הָיְתָה שֶׁלּוֹ, אֲבָל לְכָדָהּ מִמֶּלֶךְ מוֹאָב וּבְנָאָהּ לִהְיוֹת לוֹ בֵּית מַלְכוּת. וְכֵן אֲשֶׁר יוֹשֵׁב בְּעַשְׁתָּרֹת בְּאֶדְרֶעִי, שֶׁהָיְתָה אֶרֶץ רְפָאִים וְהוּא מֶלֶךְ הָאֱמֹרִי (דברים ג':ח') כַּאֲשֶׁר אֲפָרֵשׁ בעה"י (להלן ב י ג יא). וּמִפְּנֵי שֶׁאָמַר אֲשֶׁר יוֹשֵׁב בְּעַשְׁתָּרֹת בְּאֶדְרֶעִי יוֹרֶה כִּי עַשְׁתָּרוֹת שֵׁם מָקוֹם אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ אֶדְרֶעִי. וּלְשׁוֹן סִפְרֵי (דברים ד) בְּעַשְׁתָּרוֹת שֶׁהָיָה קָשֶׁה כְּעַשְׁתָּרוֹת, בְּאֶדְרֶעִי זֶה מְקוֹם מַלְכוּת. וְכָתַב רַשִׁ"י (רש"י על דברים א':ד') עַשְׁתָּרוֹת לְשׁוֹן צוּקִין וְקֹשִׁי, וְעַשְׁתָּרוֹת זֶהוּ עַשְׁתְּרוֹת קַרְנַיִם שֶׁהָיוּ בָּהּ רְפָאִים שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (בראשית יד ה) וַיַּכּוּ אֶת רְפָאִים בְּעַשְׁתְּרֹת קַרְנַיִם. בְּאֶדְרֶעִי שֵׁם מַלְכוּת, וְכֵן כָּתוּב עַשְׁתְּרוֹת צֹאנֶךָ (דברים ז':י"ג) כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ. וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ אָמְרוּ (חולין פד) לָמָּה נִקְרָא שְׁמָן עַשְׁתָּרוֹת, שֶׁמְּעַשְּׁרוֹת אֶת בַּעֲלֵיהֶן וּמְחַזְּקוֹת אוֹתָן, כָּעַשְׁתָּרוֹת הַלָּלוּ שֶׁהֵם סְלָעִים חֲזָקִים. וְהָרַב מַרְכִּיב בּוֹ שְׁתֵּי לְשׁוֹנוֹת, וְלֹא יָדַעְנוּ מֵאֵיזֶה מָקוֹם הוֹצִיא שֶׁיִּהְיֶה עַשְׁתָּרוֹת שֵׁם צוּקִין וּסְלָעִים. אֲבָל יִתָּכֵן שֶׁנֹּאמַר שֶׁהוּא שֵׁם עֶדְרֵי הַצֹּאן מִלְּשׁוֹן עֹשֶׁר כְּדִבְרֵי חֲכָמִים, וְעַשְׁתָּרוֹת קַרְנַיִם הָיוּ הָרִים גְּבוֹהִים שֶׁעֲלֵיהֶם מְצוּדוֹת סְלָעִים, יְדַמֶּה אוֹתָם הַכָּתוּב לְקַרְנֵי הַבְּהֵמוֹת כְּמוֹ שֶׁיְּדַמֶּה אוֹתָם לְשִׁנַּיִם, כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (איוב לט כח) עַל שֶׁן סֶלַע וּמְצוּדָה, וְכֵן עַל קַרְנוֹת הַמִּזְבֵּחַ (שמות כט יב), וְכֵן בְּקֶרֶן בֶּן שָׁמֶן (ישעיהו ה א), אָמַר הַתַּרְגּוּם בְּטוּר רָם בְּאַרְעָא שַׁמִּינָא. וְשָׁם יַעֲלוּ עַשְׁתְּרוֹת הַצֹּאן הַתְּיָשִׁים וְהָעִזִּים וְהַיְּעֵלִים וְכַיּוֹצֵא בָּהֶן, וּלְכָךְ יִקָּרֵא עַשְׁתְּרוֹת קַרְנַיִם. וְכֵן לַבַּעַל וְלָעַשְׁתָּרוֹת (שופטים ב יג) הע"ז הָעֲשׂוּיָה כְּצוּרַת הַצֹּאן לְהָגֵן עֲלֵיהֶם כְּפִי סִכְלוּתָם, וּבְשִׁפְלוּת הָהָר בָּנוּ עִיר וּשְׁמָהּ אֶדְרֶעִי, וְהוּא שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (דברים ג':א') וַיֵּצֵא עוֹג מֶלֶךְ הַבָּשָׁן הוּא וְכָל עַמּוֹ לַמִּלְחָמָה אֶדְרֶעִי, כִּי אָסַף אֶת כָּל חֵילוֹ אֶל הָעִיר אֲשֶׁר שָׁם אַרְמוֹן הַמֶּלֶךְ וְכִסֵּא הַמַּלְכוּת. וְעִנְיַן סִפְרֵי (שם) מִדְרָשָׁם אָמְרוּ זַ"ל אֲשֶׁר יוֹשֵׁב בְּעַשְׁתָּרֹת בְּאֶדְרֶעִי, אִלּוּ לֹא הָיָה עוֹג קָשֶׁה וְשָׁרוּי בְּעַשְׁתָּרוֹת קָשֶׁה הָיָה, שֶׁהַמְּדִינָה קָשָׁה וְכוּ', וּלְפִיכָךְ יִדְרְשׁוּ בְּעַשְׁתָּרוֹת שֶׁהָיָה קָשֶׁה כְּעַשְׁתָּרוֹת, כְּלוֹמַר שֶׁהָיָה מְקוֹם מוֹשָׁבוֹ כְּמוֹ עַשְׁתְּרוֹת קַרְנַיִם הָעִיר הַחֲזָקָה שֶׁהָיָה הוּא וּמִשְׁפַּחְתּוֹ מִשָּׁם, כִּי עַתָּה אֵינֶנּוּ יוֹשֵׁב בְּעַשְׁתָּרוֹת כִּי בְּאֶרֶץ אֱמוֹרִי הוּא יוֹשֵׁב, וּמְקוֹם מַלְכוּת כְּלוֹמַר הַמְּדִינָה שֶׁהָיָה יוֹשֵׁב בָּהּ אֶדְרֶעִי, כִּי שֵׁם אֶרֶץ מַלְכוּתוֹ הַבָּשָׁן:

AFTER HE HAD SMITTEN SIHON, THE KING OF THE AMORITES, WHO ‘DWELT’ IN HESHBON — for Heshbon was not his, but he conquered it from the king of Moab and he built it to be his royal capital. Similarly, and Og the king of Bashan, who ‘dwelt’ in Ashtaroth, at Edrei means that it was previously the land of Rephaim [and then it was occupied by the king of the Amorites] as I will explain with the help of G-d. And because Scripture states, who dwelt in Ashtaroth, at Edrei, it indicates that Ashtaroth is the name of a place in which Edrei is located [as will be explained further]. The text of the Sifre is as follows: “‘B’ashtaroth’ — it was as hard as ashtaroth. ‘B’edrei’ — this was the seat of the government [i.e., the royal city].” Rashi wrote: “Ashtaroth — is an expression denoting rocks and hardness. Ashtaroth is Ashteroth-karnaim where the Rephaim were, as it is said, and they smote the Rephaim in Ashteroth-karnaim. ‘B’edrei’ — this was the name of the kingdom [indicating that the kingdom of Edrei was located in Ashteroth-karnaim]. And so it is written, ‘ashteroth’ of thy sheep, meaning, as Targum [Onkelos] rendered it [‘the flocks of thy sheep’]. And our Rabbis have said: Why is the name ashtaroth given to them [i.e., flocks of sheep]? It is because they ‘enrich’ [from the Hebrew word ashir — rich] their owners and strengthen them like these ashtaroth which are strong rocks.” [This is Rashi’s language].Now the Rabbi [Rashi] incorporated into the word [ashtaroth] two meanings [strength and riches], but we do not know from what source the Rabbi inferred that ashtaroth is a name for rocks and stones. But it is possible for us to say that ashtaroth is a term for flocks of sheep, from the word ashir (rich) as in the words of the Sages [quoted above: “Why is their name ashtaroth? It is because they enrich their owners”]. Ashteroth-karnaim was a place of high mountains upon which there were strongholds of stone, these being likened by Scripture to “the horns of cattle,” just as Scripture likens them to “teeth,” as it says upon ‘the crag’ [literally: “the tooth”] of the rock, and the stronghold. Similarly, upon ‘the horns’ of the altar. So also, ‘b’keren’ ben shamen [literally: “in a fruitful ‘horn'”] which the Targum [Yonathan ben Uziel] renders: “On a high hill, in a fruitful land.” There, [upon these high hills,] the flocks of sheep ascend, the he-goats, the she-goats, and the wild-goats and their like; and therefore the place is called Ashteroth-karnaim [because the flocks which “enrich” their owners (ashtaroth) ascend to the “horns” of the mountain (karnaim)]. So also, and they served Baal and the Ashtaroth — ‘Ashtaroth’ because the idol was made in the form of a sheep in order to protect them [the flocks of sheep], in accordance with their foolish belief. [This is in line with our explanation of the word ashtaroth as a synonym for sheep.] Now at the foot of the mountain they built a city whose name was Edrei, this being intimated in the verse which states, and Og the king of Bashan came out against us, he and all his people, unto battle at Edrei, denoting that he gathered his entire army to the city where the palace of the king and the throne of the kingdom were. And this is the purport of the [following] Midrashic text [which seems to agree with Rashi’s interpretation], wherein the Rabbis, of blessed memory, have stated: “Who dwelt in Ashtaroth, at Edrei. Even if Og himself had not been difficult to defeat but had resided in Ashtaroth, he would have been difficult to defeat, because the city was a difficult one to capture etc.” Therefore they interpreted, Ashtaroth to mean that it was “as hard as Ashtaroth,” [the phrase from which Rashi, quoted above, deduced that the word ashtaroth is defined as “hard”], as if to say that his residence was like the fortified city of Ashteroth-karnaim from which he and his family originated; for at that time he was not residing in Ashtaroth, but was residing in the land of the Amorites. And “the place of the government” [mentioned in the Sifre above] means that the city where he lived was Edrei but Bashan was the name of the land of his kingdom.

questions.title_en: Are you allowed to drink hot chocolate before davening?
questions.question:
Are you allowed to drink hot chocolate before davening? Rabbi Belsky says no (see attached). Are there others that disagree?

CHAPTER FOUR

Do's and Don'ts Before Shacharis

Years ago, drinking coffee with milk and sugar was considered a haughty act.1 Today, this is not the case, and one is permitted to drink coffee with sugar and milk before davening if it is necessary for better concentration during davening.[2]

Hot cocoa is a rich drink made with a lot of milk, and therefore it is not permitted for adults prior to davening.[3] Children may drink hot cocoa before davening, as is a common incentive in camp.

Cappuccinos and iced coffee made with a lot of milk are not permitted either.[4] Some poskim permit soda before davening,[5] however, this should not be done.[6]

  1. Refer to Ba'er Heitev О.С. 89:11, Machatzis Hashekel 11, Chayei Adam 16:1, Sdei Chemed Rosh Hashanah page 288, Mishnah Berurah 22, Kaf Hachaim 31, Ohr L'tzion 2:7:7, Siach Tefillah page 624, Nikius V'kavod B'tefillah page 180, 104.
  2. Harav Yisroel Belsky zt"l, see Aruch Hashulchan 23, Orchos Chaim 10, Teshuvos V'hanhagos 1:73, Ketzos Hashulchan 11:2, Divrei Chachamim 4:44, Tefillah K'hilchasah 6:13 quoting Harav Elyashiv zt"l, Yalkut Yosef page 146, Minhag Yisroel Torah, Yabea Omer O.C. 4:11, Halichos Shlomo Tefillah 2:2, Oz Nidberu 11:46, Teshuros Shai 367, Keren L'Dovid 21:4, She'arim Metzuyanim B'halachah 8:2, Mivakshei Torah 3, page 248, Nishmas Avraham 1, page 53, Eretz Tzvi 2:1, Ashrei Ha'ish 1, page 97, 5, Orchos Rabbeinu 1, 181, page 57. The She'eilas Rav 2:6:43 is stringent with sugar.
  3. Harav Yisroel Belsky zt"l. See Shulchan Halevi (Hebrew) 1, page 18.
  4. Harav Yisroel Belsky zt"l.
  5. Rivevos Ephraim 8:22:2.
  6. Harav Yisroel Belsky zt"l.

questions.title_en: Why fast if the Diaspora had already been predicted?
questions.question:
While reading about Tzom Gedaliah, I was reminded of something I once learned—that the Diaspora was already foretold in the Torah. More specifically, it was indirectly hinted at as early as the 17th of Tammuz, when Moshe broke the Tablets.

Although the destruction (and following exile in Babylon and Rome) was an unspeakable tragedy, it seems that it was bound to happen eventually. If so, why do we fast? Why mourn an event that was necessary or inevitable, other than to do Teshuva?

if the events were inevitable then why should we have to fast for mistakes that were bound to happen. Perhaps because the events that would have led to the exile and the destruction of the temple could have been different, perhaps not so bloody.

questions.title_en: Would Rambam view Reform and Conservative Judaism as spiritually constructive like Christianity and Islam?
questions.question:
Rambam in Hilchos Melachim 11:4 writes that although Christianity and Islam are false religions, they nonetheless serve a role in preparing the world for the coming of Moshiach by spreading awareness of HaShem and concepts related to Torah.

Given that, would he also view Reform and Conservative Judaism as playing a similar (or better) role, by preserving some form of Jewish identity or connection that could eventually lead to teshuvah and a full embrace of Torah?

Or is their deviation from Rabbinic Torah considered more harmful than helpful, unlike Rambam's assessment of non-Jewish religions?

questions.title_en: When to write B”H or BS”D
questions.question:
There is a custom to write B”H or BS”D at the top right corner of letters. Do we need to write B”H or BS”D every time we write anything at all?

For example, do we need to write B”H or BS”D on a post-it note or while writing the contents of a box on the box itself or while making a shopping list or every page of homework etc etc?

Lets say a person needs to write the measurements of a piece of wood, on the wood itself; would he need to write B”H or BS”D first at some spot on the wood?

answers.text:
The question rightly compares Halachos (mandatory conduct) and educational practices. Many daily activities are not approved by Halachah but express spiritual aspirations.

Rambam codifies those in Hilchos Deos (Human Despositions) 3.3:

"זֶה צִוּוּ חֲכָמִים וְאָמְרוּ (משנה אבות ב יב) "וְכָל מַעֲשֶׂיךָ יִהְיוּ לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם".
וְהוּא שֶׁאָמַר שְׁלֹמֹה בְּחָכְמָתוֹ (משלי ג ו) "בְּכָל דְּרָכֶיךָ דָעֵהוּ וְהוּא יְיַשֵּׁר אֹרְחֹתֶיךָ":"
"On this matter, our Sages have directed and said (Avot 2.12):
"And all your deeds should be for the sake of Heaven."
This is what Solomon declared in his wisdom (Proverbs 3:6):
"Know Him in all your ways and He will straighten your paths".

Adding B"H or BS"D at the start of writing is purely symbolic: it reminds the writer to acknowledge Hashem as the ultimate source of wisdom and understanding, and it shows connection with the Jewish religious community.

Another example would be clothing or Peos - they both represent a level of personal adherence and communal affiliation.

Therefore, it is the writer's responsibility to determine where they draw their line.

questions.title_en: How does one choose his Rav - Do the Talmidim of Beis Shamai have an obligation to follow Beis Hillel?
questions.question:
TLDR: How does one choose a Rav in the first place? And what does one do if they listen to 2 Rabbeim that contradict one another?

Apologies for such a large post:

When the Gemara was compiled, arguably the 2 largest camps of schools of thought were Beis Shamai and Beis Hillel, and the law was decided in favor of Beis Hillel. At that point in time, did the Talmidim of Beis Shamai have an obligation to start holding like Beis Hillel as well, in direct contradiction to what their own Rabbeim told them to do?

Imagine if today, hypothetically speaking, an Ashkenazi Jew who has an Ashkenazi Rov, is told that the correct approach in life is actually Sefardi. On the one hand, he literally has his own Rebbe that he turns to and follows, and on the other hand, the law has now officially been decided opposite of his Mesorah. Do we now tell him to stop doing things in an Ashkenaz way? Is he liable to punishment for LITERALLY FOLLOWING HIS REBBE? Who has a Mesorah? What happens in that case? Because on the one hand, Mesorah is so important, and on the other hand, so is following the CORRECT Halacha?

This question deeply bothers me because there are so many differences in Yiddishkeit, so many Rabbanim saying so many things, and it seems impossible (in my humble perspective) for someone to be doing something correctly according to everyone. Ok realistically, I know there are a bunch of things we all agree on, but how is a person supposed to know they're really doing the ratzon Hashem when there are so many different shitos, hashkafos, and minhagim?

Examples:

  1. Tefillin Rashi versus Rabbeinu Tam
  2. Tefillin on Chol HaMoed or not
  3. Techeiles actually being from the Murex snail or not
  4. The myriad differences between Beis Shamai and Beis Hillel
  5. Eating Gebrukts or not on Pesach
  6. Cholov Yisroel
  7. Pas Yisroel
  8. Eating cholent on Thursday night or not
  9. Where the true international dateline is Halachically
  10. Many more Minhagim some do others don't
  11. Neitz versus Olos and Shkiah versus Tzeis (GRA vs Magen Avraham)

The point is - what is the correct way of doing something in accordance with what Hashem wants if we have differences in opinion?

How does one choose a Rov?

What if someone has many Rabbis they follow or listen to? My perspective is that why should I "nail the coffin shut" and only choose 1 Rav, if A: there is the possibility the Rav might be wrong or B: I'm fostering close mindedness by only following 1 way of Da'as Torah?

And please do not suggest asking your LOR. This question premises on trying to find which Rov or Rabbanim to follow when he doesn't have anyone that he solidly clings tightly and blindly to.

questions.title_en: Excessive details of Boaz marrying Ruth
questions.question:
Ruth 4.13 says:

"וַיִּקַּח בֹּעַז אֶת־רוּת So Boaz married Ruth;
וַתְּהִי־לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה and she became his wife,
וַיָּבֹא אֵלֶיהָ and he cohabited with her.
וַיִּתֵּן יי לָהּ הֵרָיוֹן The LORD let her conceive,
וַתֵּלֶד בֵּן׃ and she bore a son."

What explains such a level of specificity?

answers.text: Because Boaz was extremely old, he had no sons previously, and he was only alive with Ruth a short amount of time. Someone may say that Boaz was not the father. Some may say that the marriage was invalid. So the Megillah emphasizes all of steps to enforce that they are real and good.

Malbim has a clever reading: there is actual Yibum -- marrying the widow of one's deceased, childless brother -- and then there is quasi-Yibum: in the spirit of the law of Yibum, having other family members marry the widow to carry on the name.

As Boaz was a cousin, this was in-the-spirt-of Yibum, not actual Yibum.

In real Yibum, a marriage ceremony is (technically) not required -- they just move in together. (The rabbis later added a for-show ceremony, for obvious reasons.) In a sense, it's that the first brother's marriage never really ended, and just transferred to the living brother.

So the verse is stressing that this was quasi-Yibum. It required proper marriage ("he took her", and then she became his wife) before cohabitation.

An alternative suggestion -- the narrator notes that by the end of the book, Naomi was walking around with baby Oved, and the townspeople are saying, "hey look, Naomi's new baby!". So the narrator is making sure that future generations understand that the actual mother of the baby was, in fact, Ruth.

questions.title_en: Understanding the ending of Ruth - Naomi's benefits, Oved's name, and the memory of Mahlon
questions.question:
Please, help me understand the ending of the Book of Ruth (4.10-17). For convenience, I grouped several questions in one here:

  1. "And may your house be like the house of Perez whom Tamar bore to Judah—
    through the offspring which the LORD will give you by this young woman     -
    The whole point of Perez's lineage was King David. What was special about the house of Perez (except for being born "in sin") for Oved to be likened backward to?
  2. "And the women said to Naomi, 'Blessed be the LORD, who has not withheld a redeemer from you today!'... He will renew your life and sustain your old age; for he is born of your daughter-in-law, who loves you and is better to you than seven sons. " -
    The ending glorifies Naomi and presents Boaz's acquisition as Naomi's benefit. What does she have to do with the move? How does she profit from the deal?
  3. "Naomi took the child and held it to her bosom. She became its foster mother, and the women neighbors gave him a name, saying, “A son is born to Naomi!” They named him Obed; he was the father of Jesse, the father of David." -
    The child, Obed, was born to Ruth and Boaz. What does he have to do with Naomi to be considered her son? Why did the neighbor women give him the name - what kind of practice is this? Why doesn't the text tell how Boaz named his son upon circumcision

Maybe a stand-alone question:
4. "I am also acquiring Ruth the Moabite, the wife of Mahlon, as my wife, so as to perpetuate the name of the deceased upon his estate, that the name of the deceased may not disappear from among his kinsmen and from the gate of his home town. -
Doesn't "perpetuate the name of the deceased that his name may not disappear" mean that the child will be called after Mahlon and Elimelech, rather than Boaz? Otherwise, how didn't Mahlon's name disappear?

questions.title_en: Balak's Messengers - multiple titles
questions.question:
From what I can see, the messengers that Balak sends are referred to, in the same few verses, using multiple different titles. First they are called the Elders (of Midian - Bamidbar 22:4), then "messengers" (ibid 5), then the Elders of Moab and the Elders of Midian (ibid 7) then the Princes of Balak (ibid 13), then the Princes of Moab (ibid 13), then the servants of Balak (ibid 18), then "the men" (anashim - ibid 20), and then the Princess of Moab again (ibid 21).

I understand there are commentaries on each verse, for example Ibn Ezra on ibid 13 says that they are the Princess of Balak specifically (and not Moab) to indicate that he was the protagonist of sending them, but is anyone aware of a more general, comprehensive discussion on why the verses refer to them in so many different ways across the chapter?

questions.title_en: Did Chava eat the fruit before or after Adam?
questions.question:
A simple reading would imply the serpent convinced Chava to eat first, and she did so because she was caught up in his words at the time. Then, she gave it to Adam.

But Rashi says that she gave it to Adam because she was worried that if she passed away and not him, then he would marry another woman.

Does Rashi suggest that Chava gave the fruit to Adam first?

answers.text: Im not sure your implication. She was scared she would pass away since she ate from it. Since she didn't want him to marry another woman she therefore gave him to eat so if she dies so does he.

There is nothing in the verse itself (Bereishit 3:6) that suggests that she gave it to Adam to eat first. That verse reads:

וַתֵּ֣רֶא הָֽאִשָּׁ֡ה כִּ֣י טוֹב֩ הָעֵ֨ץ לְמַאֲכָ֜ל וְכִ֧י תַֽאֲוָה־ה֣וּא לָעֵינַ֗יִם וְנֶחְמָ֤ד הָעֵץ֙ לְהַשְׂכִּ֔יל וַתִּקַּ֥ח מִפִּרְי֖וֹ וַתֹּאכַ֑ל וַתִּתֵּ֧ן גַּם־לְאִישָׁ֛הּ עִמָּ֖הּ וַיֹּאכַֽל׃ When the woman saw that the tree was good for eating and a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was desirable as a source of wisdom, she took of its fruit and ate. She also gave some to her husband, and he ate.

Further, there is nothing in Rashi's words that would specifically lend an interpretation that runs contrary to that interpretation, that should cause us to revisit that assumption. Rashi wrote:

ותתן גם לאישה. שֶׁלֹּא תָמוּת הִיא וְיִחְיֶה הוּא, וְיִשָּׂא אַחֶרֶת: ותתן גם לאשה AND SHE GAVE ALSO TO HER HUSBAND so that she should not die and he remain alive to take another wife (Genesis Rabbah 19:5).

The idea could very well be that, after eating, she reflected and decided that she should give to her husband. Such contemplation that she would die is not something that she would do and then, despite that, eat it! It would be after eating and having regrets, now that she realizes the repercussions.

Indeed, Rashi seldom innovates his own interpretations to Torah. Instead, he "channels" existing midrashim. In Bereishit Rabba 19:5, this appears as:

וַתִּקַּח מִפִּרְיוֹ וַתֹּאכַל (בראשית ג, ו), אָמַר רַבִּי אַיְבוּ סָחֲטָה עֲנָבִים וְנָתְנָה לוֹ, רַבִּי שִׂמְלָאי אָמַר בְּיִשּׁוּב הַדַּעַת בָּאת עָלָיו, אָמְרָה לֵיהּ מַה אַתָּה סָבוּר שֶׁאֲנִי מֵתָה וְחַוָּה אַחֶרֶת נִבְרֵאת לְךָ (קהלת א, ט): אֵין כָּל חָדָשׁ תַּחַת הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ, אוֹ שֶׁמָּא אֲנִי מֵתָה וְאַתְּ יוֹשֵׁב לְךָ הַטְלִיס, (ישעיה מה, יח): לֹא תֹהוּ בְרָאָהּ לָשֶׁבֶת יְצָרָהּ, רַבָּנָן אָמְרֵי הִתְחִילָה מְיַלֶּלֶת עָלָיו בְּקוֹלָהּ

She took from its fruit and ate” – Rabbi Aivu said: She squeezed grapes and gave it to him [Adam]. Rabbi Simlai said: She came to him persuasively. She said to him: ‘What, do you think that I will die and another Eve will be created for you? “There is nothing new under the sun” (Ecclesiastes 1:9). Or, perhaps [you think that] I will die and you will sit alone? “He did not create it [the world] for emptiness, He formed it to be inhabited”’ (Isaiah 45:18). The Rabbis say: She began sobbing at him plaintively with her voice.

This reads fairly clearly as her already facing death, for having eaten it, and now trying to convince Adam to eat as well.

questions.title_en: Could Chiram be a Descendant of a Child That Samson Conceived with Plishti, Married Women While Incarcerated?
questions.question:
The Talmud in Sota (10a) states that Plishti men brought their wives to Samson while he was in jail to conceive:

״וַיְהִי טוֹחֵן בְּבֵית הָאֲסוּרִים״. אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: אֵין טְחִינָה אֶלָּא לְשׁוֹן עֲבֵירָה, וְכֵן הוּא אוֹמֵר: ״תִּטְחַן לְאַחֵר אִשְׁתִּי״. מְלַמֵּד שֶׁכׇּל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד הֵבִיא לוֹ אֶת אִשְׁתּוֹ לְבֵית הָאֲסוּרִים כְּדֵי שֶׁתִּתְעַבֵּר הֵימֶנּוּ. With regard to Samson’s capture, the verse states: “... and he did grind in the prison-house” (Judges 16:21). Rabbi Yoḥanan says: Grinding is nothing other than a language of a transgression of sexual intercourse, and so the verse says: “Then let my wife grind unto another man” (Job 31:10). This teaches that each and every Philistine man brought his wife to the prison in order that she should be impregnated by Samson.

Divrei Hayamim 2 3,17 states:

וַיָּ֤קֶם אֶת־הָֽעַמּוּדִים֙ עַל־פְּנֵ֣י הַהֵיכָ֔ל אֶחָ֥ד מִיָּמִ֖ין וְאֶחָ֣ד מֵֽהַשְּׂמֹ֑אול וַיִּקְרָ֤א שֵׁם־[הַיְמָנִי֙] (הימיני) יָכִ֔ין וְשֵׁ֥ם הַשְּׂמָאלִ֖י בֹּֽעַז׃ {ס}         He erected the columns in front of the Great Hall, one to its right and one to its left; the one to the right was called Jachin, and the one to the left, Boaz.

Rashi on Divrei Hayamim 2 3,17 states:

ד"א חירם שהיה מבני דן עשה את העמודים קרא את האחד יכין על שם אביו שמשון שנאמר בו (שופטים ט״ז:כ״ח-כ״ט) וילפת שמשון שני עמודי התוך (וגו' נכון וגו') ושלמה קרא לשני בועז Another explanation: Huram, who was one of the sons of Dan, made the pillars. He called one Jachin after his father Samson, about whom Scripture states (Jud. 16:29): “And Samson grasped the two pillars of the center, etc.” And Solomon called the second one Boaz after his grandfather, Boaz.

I see three possibilities here:

  1. Samson was the honorary father of everyone in Dan. He has no actual genetic connection to Chiram.
  2. Chiram descends from one of Samson's Jewish offspring. Per the Rambam, Samson converted his wife(s). The challenge here is that there is no mention of children in connection with any of the three women he encountered.
  3. Perhaps, Chiram descends from a child of one of the non-Jewish Plishtim that Samson had relations with in jail, * and said child (or decendant) subsequently converted to Judaism.*

*Does the third possibility - the tribe of Dan redux - work?

answers.text:
The Chiram referred to here (called Chiram/Chirom in Melachim, and Churam in Divrei HaYamim) is an Israelite who built the Temple, who lived in Tyre, from the tribes of Naftali and Dan. Not to be confused with King Chiram of Tyre, who was also involved in the building of the Temple.

Here is how (Pseudo-)Rashi explains his lineage (Divrei HaYamim 2:13):

ואביו איש צורי - יהודי היה יושב בצור דוגמא עובד אדום הגתי (שמואל ב' ו) שהיה יושב בגת ולוי היה ובמלכים (א ז) כתיב ובן אשה אלמנה ממטה נפתלי ואביו איש צורי אלא אמו מדן ואביו מנפתלי ומה צריך לייחס מאיזה שבט היה אביו ואמו זהו שכתוב (בראשית ל') דנני אלהים וגם נפתולי אלהים וגו' (שם) אמרה רחל מעתה עקמתי פתולים עקמומיות עשיתי עד שאני יכולה לדמות עצמי ללאה אחותי אם לאה תתפאר בבצלאל בנה שיעשה המשכן יצטרך להשתתף במלאכתו אחד מבני דן שנאמר ואתו אהליאב בן אחיסמך למטה דן ואם שלמה בן אחותי יבנה ב"ה צריך להשתתף עמו מבני דן ונפתלי

So this Chiram was descended from Dan on his mother's side. And so the (Pseudo-)Rashi you quote surmises that he may have been descended from Shimshon, as an attempt to explain the choice of the name Yachin for the pillar.

questions.title_en: Why are Gil'ad's children considered their own family?
questions.question:
In Bamidbar (26:30-32), the children of Gil'ad, son of Machir ben Menasheh, are mentioned as heads of their own families. Every other time a grandson of one of the twelve tribes is called their own family, Rashi (26:24, 26:36) explains why: either because they were born before Ya'akov went to Mitzrayim, or because they were fathers of exceptionally large families.

However, when it comes to the six sons of Gil'ad, Rashi doesn't explain why they're considered separate families. What makes this even stranger is the fact that these are the only great-grandchildren considered heads of their own families! (Also, per Rashi, the only reason Gil'ad is mentioned is because he had a large family, so further "watering down" the families into smaller groups seems counterintuitive).

So why were these great-grandchildren considered their own families, and why didn't Rashi explain it?

questions.title_en: Ambiguous references to Talmudic sages
questions.question: Sanhedrin 17b explains a list of terms used to refer to certain Talmudic sages. There are pretty straightforward ones, like רַבּוֹתֵינוּ שֶׁבְּבָבֶל: רַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל (our teachers in Babylonia: Rav and Shemueil) or דַּיָּינֵי דְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל: רַבִּי אַמִּי וְרַבִּי אַסִּי (the judges of the Land of Israel: R' Ami and R' Assi). However, there are plenty others where a plural expression refers to a single person, like רַבּוֹתֵינוּ שֶׁבְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל: רַבִּי אַבָּא (our teachers in the Land of Israel: R' Abba). How come? Why did they use a term in plural to denote a single person?

questions.title_en: Who is Rabbi Abba bar Mimi
questions.question: As mentioned here https://library.alhatorah.org/?r1=Shir_HaShirim_Rabbah_1:10 in Shir HaShirim Rabbah, this Rabbi Abba bar Mimi is given as the prime example of someone who would discuss and debate Halacha with his friends. Who exactly is this rabbi? A quick concordance search shows no other results for him anywhere else except for here. And is Mimi his mother’s name?

answers.text:
According to Rav Aharon Hyman in Toledot Tannaim vaAmoraim, this is his sole occurrence. Rav Hyman also cites Rav Yerucham Leiner in Seder HaDorot HaShalem, that in Rosh HaShanah 35a, which reads:

כִּי סְלֵיק רַבִּי אַבָּא מִיַּמֵּי, פֵּירְשַׁהּ: מוֹדִים חֲכָמִים לְרַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל בִּבְרָכוֹת שֶׁל רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה וְשֶׁל יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים, וַהֲלָכָה מִכְּלָל דִּפְלִיגִי בִּבְרָכוֹת דְּכׇל הַשָּׁנָה.

The Gemara answers: When Rabbi Abba returned from his travels at sea, he explained the matter as follows: The Sages concede to the opinion of Rabban Gamliel with regard to the blessings of Rosh HaShana and of Yom Kippur, that in these cases the prayer leader fulfills the obligation on behalf of the many. And Rabbi Yoḥanan’s statement that the halakha is in accordance with Rabban Gamliel, which, by inference, indicates that the tanna’im still disagree, is referring to the blessings of the entire year.

that perhaps instead of reading מימי as מִיַּמֵּי, from the Seas (which Rashi explains as שהפליג בספינה לים וחזר, that Rabbi Abba set out by boat to sea and returned), that we should read it as a single name with a missing "bar", such that it is Rabbi Abba bar Mimi.

I examined various manuscripts on Hachi Garsinan and, while there are several variants, none are bar Mimi.

In terms of Mimi being his mother, there is no reason to make such an assumption, even though Mimi is a female name in modern times. The default assumption should be that this is his father's name.

questions.title_en: Did Napoleon come to Jerusalem and want to rebuild the temple?
questions.question:
I heard one Rav said that Napoleon came to Jerusalem and saw us lamenting the destruction of the Temple and wanted to rebuild it, however the rabbis said no.

Is that reported elsewhere?

answers.text:
Responding to the title question, Napoleon was not able to reach Jerusalem during his campaign in the Land of Israel. Famously, he laid siege on Acre (Akko) in 1799, but lost, and from there backtracked to Egypt (for a short summary of his time in the Land of Israel, see here). So at least that part of the story isn't true.

However, there were a couple of instances during his reign where he said things that were either explicitly related to the Temple or could be hinted at that. First, he had pre-prepared a proclamation to be announced in Jerusalem after he captured it, where he would have proclaimed the Land of Israel (Palestine in his words) a Jewish state. Such autonomy would likely have allowed the Jews to rebuild the Temple. In 1800, Napoleon declared: "If I governed a nation of Jews, I should reestablish the Temple of Solomon." (source; see here for the full quote and the original French).

So these are indications that Napoleon at a time was interested in rebuilding the Temple, as he saw that as the best way to gain favor in the eyes of the Jews. Having failed in the Land of Israel, however, he chose a different practical and ideological approach: the French Emancipation of the Jews. There are certain arguments to be made that at some point he shifted more into an ideological direction of attempting to redefine the Jewish belief in the redemption as something surrounding himself (as the messianic figure) and France (as the New Jerusalem), and the Emancipation as the Jewish Redemption (Geulah) (see here for info). Thus, for example, he established the Grand Sanhedrin which was mainly intended to give supposed Jewish halachic legitimacy to the emancipation. If you look at the topics discussed by the Grand Sanhedrin, you'll see that one of their decisions was announcing that Jews should see their birthplace as their fatherland. This was of course important in establishing primacy of French identity over Jewish identity (with the hopes of similar views spreading across Europe during a time when it was believed Napoleon would be able to conquer at least all of the West), solidifying the view that France was the new Jerusalem and the new Land of Israel.

questions.title_en: May mourners take their children out to have fun during sheloshim?
questions.question: When someone dies, the siblings must observe sheloshim. But what about their children? Sure, sheloshim is obligatory only on the siblings themselves, but they are the ones who would take their children to amusement parks, movies, vacation spots, and other forms of entertainment, especially in the summertime. Are they allowed to do that?

answers.text:
R Simcha Bunim Cohen in his book The laws of aveilus (pp. 224) partly answers your question

One is permitted to take a trip with immediate family members (i.e., parents with their children).

A mourner may participate in a joyful activity of a young child who is incapable of comprehending and accepting the concept that the mourning parent cannot participate. However, the parent's participation should be limited to what is required. When music is being played the parent should avoid listening to it as much as possible (i.e., by using earplugs or by not paying attention).

questions.question:
Why does the Torah call a person from "מצרים", a מצרי instead of a מצרימי?

Is it because the second-to-last letter is a yud? Or does it have to do with the origin of the name? Or maybe something else?

answers.text:
The Malbim (style) Haggadah (s.v. עבדים היינו לפרעה) explains:

השם מצרים אינו שם עצם סתם בלי טעם, כמו "ירושלים", דאז היה נגזר היחס בשם מצרימי ומצרימים, ומה שנגזר בשם "מצרי", זה מורה ש"מצרים" הוא שם הקיבוץ, ורוצה לומר מדינה קשה של מצירים ומעיקים רבים.

This is also cited in Sefer Hacarmel, (מצרים).

The name Egypt is not a mere noun without meaning, in which case the relation would be derived from the name מצרימי and מצרימים. The reason we use "מצרי", is because it is derived from מצרים, which refers to the collective, and is intended to convey that it was a difficult country of many oppressors.

One of the ancient Egyptian names for “Egypt” was taʀwai, which literally means ”two lands”, referring to the fact that it was split into two districts—the north and the south.

When we came to Egypt, we loan-translated that endonym into Hebrew as miṣraim (“two countries”), from the stem m-ṣ-r (literally “border”)¹. Because that stem was rare in Hebrew, its main usage became that regarding Egypt, so that it eventually connoted specifically Egypt by default.

The word miṣrī, therefore, meant “countryman”, and almost exclusively connoted a specifically Egyptian countryman.

Theoretically, if the Egyptian word for “Egypt” were somehow miṣraim, we might very well have considered it a base noun without parsing it into miṣr and the dual suffix, and our word for “Egyptian” would’ve been miṣraimī. But that’s not what Ancient Egyptian word was, so this isn’t what happened.

(Note that this answer explains the historical origins of the Hebrew words for Egypt and its people, and is not an exegesis. @IsraelReader’s answer offers a wonderful exegesis.)

¹Possibly influenced by c’Vrwai or c’Vraw, meaning “[two] borders”.

questions.title_en: Did anyone challenge the Radzyner's techeiles on the basis of the definiton of chilazon?
questions.question:
R' Benzion Halberstam gives a very interesting shiur discussing some of the proofs in favor of the Murex trunculus and disproving some of the arguments against it. He discusses the Radzyner's shittah as well.

During the shiur, he addresses, among other points:

  1. The definition of chilazon as a snail, quoting many rishonim who use terms that clearly identify the chilazon as a snail/worm.
  2. The argument against the Murex relating to a lack of mesorah. During this portion he explains that the inyan of mesorah as it relates to concepts in halachah is important vis-a-vis definitions, i.e. knowing what a word means based on a definition passed through generations as opposed to defining a term by sevarah. He says that it's important to have definitions passed through generations, and he says that part of the challenge to the Radzyner's techeiles is that he attempted to define חלזון by sevara rather than by שאל אביך ויגדך, by mesorah.

My questions are as follows. If the definition of חלזון is so clearly passed through the generations to mean "snail"/"worm" based on the opinions of many mainstream rishonim,

  1. How did the Radzyner come to conclude that it was a cuttlefish, which is clearly not a snail; and
  2. Did anyone challenge his conclusion on the basis of those rishonim who describe the חלזון as a snail/worm?

answers.text:
The Radziner Rebbe expanded the word chilazon to include other creatures that have an encasement (nartik), but there is no doubt that even according to him, the murex is a species of chilazon.

Definitely, many rabbonim did not agree to his identification because of the points you brought. See for example Yeshuot Malko where the Radziner’s claims about identifying the chilazon are described as ‘nothing but mere supposition’ (Sec. 2) and ‘nothing but conjecture’ (Sec. 3).

Interestingly, he did check with zoologists who may have told him that the cuttlefish is from the mollusc family, so he may have thought that was enough to qualify it as a chilazon.

questions.title_en: Learn to translate Chumash
questions.question: I'd like to learn how to translate Chumash, not needing to look at translation. I need to expand my vocabulary. I have already studied grammar. I learnt that kids in school learn this in 2 years. Can anyone recommend a series of practice books to get me there. Even if its a kids book, but you learned from it, or your kid learned from it. Please only speak out of experience.

answers.text:
Rabbi Jonathan Rietti has a very structured program for learning to translate the words in the Torah. From his website:

Of the 16,000 words in Chumash Bereishis, 80% are variations of the same 303 root-words. When these 303 shorashim are combined with a working knowledge of the Prefixes/Suffixes, the student will be able to independently translate over 80% of the words in Chumash Bereishis.

I haven't used the program myself, but having gone through a formal yeshiva education that implemented a similar method of learning Hebrew I can attest to the importance of a structure like this.

I found the following two books to be extremely helpful. First of all they are focused on the Hebrew of the Chumash, not modern Hebrew. Second they are extremely pedagogical and take you through the learning step by step. Third they include large amounts of vocabulary to increase independence in translation. Very highly recommended.

  • The Guide To Lashon Hakodesh, Vol 1: Mastering the Basics
  • The Guide to Lashon Hakodesh, Volume 2: Mastering Hebrew Verbs

In addition, you will likely benefit from learning lists of frequently occurring words in Chumash, such as this list.

questions.title_en: How can a Jewish store sell a gift card at a discount, isn’t that a problem of Ribbis. A gift card is really a loan as it gives the store capital now?
questions.question: How can a Jewish store sell a gift card at a discounted price. A gift card is a loan that provides capital to the to store at the time of purchase of the gift card. So this should be Ribbis?

answers.text:
Generally speaking, Ribbis involves charging for allowing someone to use your money for a given amount of time (אגר נטר).

Since the person buying the gift card could use the gift card today, for its entire value, there is no time component here, and hence there is no transgression of Ribbis.

See Shulchan Aruch Harav (Hilchos Ribbis, 23) that in a case where the vendor has goods to sell (יש לו סחורה), at the time of receipt of the money, there is not even a prohibition of אבק ריבית.

questions.title_en: Dikduk question about word in Hadran
questions.question:
The text of the Hadran contains the sentence: וּזְכוּת כָּל הַתַּנָּאִים וְהָאֲמוֹרָאִים וְתַלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים יַעֲמֹד לִי וּלְזַרְעִי שֶׁלֹּא תָּמוּשׁ הַתּוֹרָה מִפִּי וּמִפִּי זַרְעִי עַד עוֹלָם

questions.title_en: Was the land of Israel private property or collective
questions.question:
I’m curious as to who the land belonged to. As far as I know the Land belonged to God then the tribes. The sages or kings if they could then confiscate land etc if needed. But it never truly belonged to anyone.

Meaning you could never sell the land to another forever, the land d was Gods and given to the Hebrews to keep.

Maybe my understanding is wrong?

answers.text:
A Covenantal Stewardship Rather than Absolute Ownership

The Land of Israel was conceived as a unique blend of private stewardship and collective ownership under God. On one hand, each Israelite family received its own portion of land – there was a concept of private property and inheritance. On the other hand, that ownership was never absolute: it was circumscribed by God’s commandments and the community’s welfare. Rabbi Hirsch’s commentary on Deuteronomy 8:11 highlights the spiritual truth behind this arrangement:

Through Birkat Hamazon, the consciousness should always be kept awake to whom WE owe the land and its blessings, under what conditions and for what purpose we receive it, that we remain worthy of the received blessings only as long as we remain mindful of the obligation that renews with every received divine gift, to become a "blessing" ourselves, a blessing of God's work, fulfillers of the divine will on earth. Beware lest you forget, for it is precisely the abundance that could make us forget God. (Deuteronomy 8:10-11)

The Land of Israel in Jewish law was neither a purely private commodity nor a free-for-all collective in the modern sense, but something higher: a holy inheritance held in trust as we see in Zohar I 83a (15:144-145):

The inner meaning of this story is: Had Abram not descended to Egypt and been tested there, his portion would not have been with HaShem. Likewise, his descendants, whom HaShem wanted to make into a unique and perfect nation and bring close: Had they not first descended to Egypt and been tested there, they would not have become HaShem's chosen people. Similarly, the Holy Land: Had it not first been given to Canaan for dominion, it would not have become the lot and portion of the Holy One, blessed be He.

Therefore, each person’s plot was a piece of the national patrimony under God’s domain, with the entire people responsible for each other and for the land itself. The divine rules of ownership ensured that the land’s benefits were shared and sustained collectively – whether through mandatory charity from the harvest, communal rest for the soil, or restrictions on harmful farming practices as we see in Mishnah Bava Kamma 7:7:

One may not raise small domesticated animals, i.e., sheep and goats, in settled areas of Eretz Yisrael, as they graze on people’s crops. But one may raise them in Syria, despite the fact that with regard to many other halakhot Syria is treated like Eretz Yisrael, and in the wilderness of Eretz Yisrael.

questions.title_en: Brain death as Halachic death - revisited

questions.title_en: Is there such a thing as reverse Sechita (the Dilatancy effect)?
questions.question:
Is Sechita strictly speaking the act of squeezing/wringing a material whereby liquid emerges as a result, or does Sechita include the opposite act, wherein a liquid emerges from the material when a force is no longer applied (also known as the Dilatancy effect)?

For example, there is a phenomenon by moist sand that by squeezing the sand together, the pressure actually increases the space between the sand molecules, causing any surrounding liquid to be absorbed more, and when letting go of that same clump, the liquid then starts to get released. It acts counterintuitively, since you would expect that the normal act of squeezing should force liquid out, and the act of letting go should cause more liquid to go back into the clump. But sand does the opposite.

So does squeezing sand on Shabbos, aside from the issue of forming or kneading, also incur Sechita?

questions.title_en: What is the history of the search for the chilazon?
questions.question:
In the past century and a half, there have been two attempts to find the chilazon. One, the Radzyner Rebbe's, was never widely accepted and is viewed to have been conclusively disproven. The other, the Murex trunculus, has significant supporters and detractors.

I was listening to a shiur series by R' Mordechai Hershfeld about proofs for and against these two attempts to procure the techeiles. One argument he makes against the Murex in particular is the inyan of nignaz (which he discusses in three parts) - essentially arguing that chilazon will not reemerge until the time of the Moshiach. To me that rung untrue because no one's argument against the Radzyner was "nignaz."

This whole train of thought led me to wonder - had there been any other attempts throughout history, however unsuccessful, to find the chilazon?

answers.text:
Rav Yitzchak Isaac Halevi Herzog spent much time in attempting to identify the chilazon, writing his PhD thesis on the topic.

His preferred candidate was, in fact, neither of the two you listed in the question, but rather a different genus of sea snail, janthina.

The Radbaz and others were already with the idea that they could find the chilazon any time. This matches the idea that in the 16th century there was a high messianic fervour, so the restoration of techelet is a necessity and harbinger of the redemption.

But no formal candidates were ever proposed perhaps because whoever really knew about it mentioned that it was the porphyra, although they might not have been able to precisely gotten their hands on it or try to experiment with it.

Until the fall of Constantinople, there was a formal ban to use any murex trunculus in the lands of the Byzantine and Holy Roman Empire. As the empire fell you see acharonim all the sudden talking about the chilazon and even identifying it with the porphyra, aka murex trunculus.

So it could be well that we all knew along which animal was but we did not dare to write it down due to fear of repression or censorship. The Ramban clearly stated that the chilazon was in power of the Melech Goyim and no one would dare to wear it, so it is possible that any open discussion of the identify was frown upon too.
